On a special edition of Washington Week With The Atlantic , the Atlantic staff writer Josh Tyrangiel joined for a discussion about the future of AI and what, if anything, the U.S. government plans to do to address the rapid development of the technology

Across the country, massive data centers are being built, and they’re “landing themselves without a whole lot of conversation” in American towns, Tyrangiel said last night. “It’s natural that all the fears about AI—about it taking your jobs, about it rendering human beings obsolete, about the values it changes—all are focused on” these data centers, he argued. “And politicians have been incredibly late to wake up to the anger around AI.” “I don’t think people believe that they are going to partake in the wealth that comes from data centers in their community,” Tyrangiel continued. “Every community is going to make different choices, but what I’m sensing is that, particularly from Trump, the politics are out of line with where people are.” Watch Tyrangial’s full conversation with the editor in chief of The Atlantic , Jeffrey Goldberg, here .

title: Rediscover the Ordinary

body: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning
A strange thing happens when you see something every day: Eventually, you stop seeing it
A building you once admired becomes part of your commute
The trees on your block become background
Your favorite coffee mug becomes something you reach for without thinking

This tendency has been compounded by a culture that encourages us to move through life as efficiently as possible: We follow directions instead of wandering, put in headphones instead of listening to the world around us, and fill spare moments by looking at our phone
As Ian Bogost writes in a new article, we’ve become so focused on making life more productive that we risk treating the present as mere preparation for whatever comes next
Wonder can interrupt that habit, Bogost argues—not just the kind inspired by mountains or sunsets, but the kind available in ordinary things
He describes noticing the warmth of a coffee mug, the crunch of gravel underfoot, and the clever engineering of a toaster
Wonder, in this sense, is less about seeking out extraordinary experiences than it is about paying close attention to the ones already around you

title: Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
excerpt: Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach
body: Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach
When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing
He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light
And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk
Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention
He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him
The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf
This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s
Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring
After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request

He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post. [ From the February 1991 issue: Out of your car, off your horse ] A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr
Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone

When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter
I’d asked him to take part in “ By Heart ,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook
He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World , contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way
It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself
Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk
And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since
I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible
Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written

Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorrow” seemed to better describe the ethos of Berry’s longtime nemeses: coal-industry strip miners, big agribusiness, the global financial system
It was also an odd choice for someone who seemed so concerned about the excesses of modern life
Berry struck me as someone who absolutely would fixate on the general worsening direction of things
Fretting about the future is a favorite preoccupation of the conscientious

Berry occasionally admitted to his own worried state of mind on the page, including in one of his best-known poem s : “When despair for the world grows in me,” he wrote, “I wake in the night at the least sound / in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be.” Nevertheless, in the part of his book that he asked me to read, he wrote, “Taking thought for the morrow is, fairly predictably, a waste of time.” He insisted that what we call “the future” is a flimsy and insubstantial thing at best—a phantom we obsess over that never really arrives, or never arrives in the way we imagine. “Most of the bad possibilities I have worried about have never happened,” Berry wrote. “By taking thought for the morrow we have invested, and wasted, a lot of effort in preparing for morrows that never came.” Obsessing about the future, he argued, also has devastating moral consequences
It allows people to avoid engaging with the urgent realities of the present
I don’t know whether Berry, given his extremely offline lifestyle, ever learned about doomscrolling—the way social media can serve as a collective orgy of dread

But he’s right that, when people become too obsessed with a future that may or may not befall them, they tend to turn their back on the moment they’re in. “The time is coming when it will be too late to save the world
Oh, oh, oh,” he wrote, lampooning the handwringer in so many of us. “If that is the way our minds are afflicted, we and our world are dead already
The present is going by and we are not in it.” As I see it, this was the core purpose of Berry’s work: He dared his readers to live in a way that honors the situation at hand, at this very second
That mandate suffused everything he wrote about
He exhorted readers to enjoy the food on their plates, to bear witness to the places that surround them, and to revel in shared experience with the people in their orbit
Honoring the present was a joyful thing for Wendell Berry
It was also a form of rewarding but very difficult work
It meant slow, careful deliberation about the things he was willing to let into his life, whether that was a new piece of technology or a request from a journalist
And it meant searching for ways to disentangle himself, by turns and sometimes painfully, from destructive systems
The moral goal of a human being, he often argued, should be to do less harm right now

When one of his most famous essays, 1987’s “ Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer ,” resulted in astonished and outraged letters from readers, Berry replied by writing, “I did not say that I proposed to end forthwith all my involvement in harmful technology, for I do not know how to do that

I said merely that I want to limit such involvement, and to a certain extent I do know how to do that.” This response boils down to a simple, radical worldview: We must seek to understand the harms caused by the systems we’re implicated in, then strive to become less reliant on them. [ From the February 1992 issue: A jonquil for Mary Penn ] Berry was no purist
He understood that no 20th- or 21st-century American can live a wholly blameless life

title: J. D. Vance’s Disingenuous Defense of Tucker Carlson
excerpt: Vance was asked at a press conference on Thursday about his relationship with Tucker Carlson, the media personality and ultra-right-wing conspiracy theorist, he
body: Vance was asked at a press conference on Thursday about his relationship with Tucker Carlson, the media personality and ultra-right-wing conspiracy theorist, he displayed a surprising side of himself: human, vulnerable, almost touchingly naive. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them
I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go

And if you have a disagreement with somebody politically, even over a deeply held issue, you should still be friends with that person, because the whole republic depends on people of different perspectives being able to talk to one another.” This was a matter not of politics, Vance was at pains to emphasize, but of friendship

If Vance were to renounce Carlson over a matter as trivial as, say, Carlson’s oddly positive assessment of Adolf Hitler, what hope is there for society? The bonds of affection between Vance and Carlson are the very glue holding together the American experiment
And yet, tempting though it might be to imagine Vance clasping hands with the children of the world and teaching them to sing in perfect harmony, some notes of skepticism are warranted
Perhaps Vance’s affection for Carlson has more to do with holding the loyalty of his friend’s enormous audience. [ Peter Wehner: What J
Vance once knew ] For one, Vance is not known for cordially disagreeing with people

He has accumulated an unusual number of bitter enemies by flinging insults at people—including Senate Democrats (“You’re full of shit, and everyone knows it”), reporters (“scumbags”), and “childless cat ladies.” Last month, Vance hurled himself into an obscure debate over burrito prices to make a gratuitous swipe at a conservative Washington Post columnist’s weight

At the very same press conference where he waxed so earnestly about open dialogue, Vance mocked the idea that he would talk to former President Biden at the 9/11 ceremony (“I’m really looking forward to hanging out with Joe Biden

I’m sure that we’ll have many, many intense intellectual conversations, and it’ll be great”) and dismissed the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as “a crazy person.” Vance’s dig at El-Sayed, and the context in which he made it, revealed a lot more about his reasons for maintaining the alliance with Carlson than did his encomium to friendship
Vance was trying to illustrate that he and Carlson do not agree on everything
Carlson had recently praised El-Sayed as “America First” and “literally Trumpian,” apparently calculating that the candidate’s anti-Zionism outweighs his many left-wing positions
That view was the one Vance chose to highlight as his point of disagreement, rather than several other controversial remarks Carlson has made

Examples include but are not limited to his endorsement of “Great Replacement” and other conspiracy theories, his expressions of sympathy for Russia and its war against Ukraine, and his sympathetic interviews with figures such as Nick Fuentes, Alex Jones, and the World War II–revisionist historian Darryl Cooper, who called Winston Churchill “the chief villain of the Second World War” and described much of the Holocaust as mistaken deaths resulting from poor planning
All of these statements have left Carlson teetering at the edge of respectability within the Republican Party
He has become one of the most prominent exponents of a strain of right-wing populism that flirts with and in some cases embraces isolationism, anti-Semitism, and general crackpottery
Vance has courted this faction of the right
He and Carlson have a partnership that has lasted nearly a decade and has yielded dozens of interviews
In the course of this partnership, they may well have formed a genuine friendship
But Vance has discarded plenty of friends as he has cycled through various political identities
The difference between Vance’s ex-friends and Carlson is that Carlson is still a useful ally in a Republican factional conflict

When Carlson upset Fox News in 2021 by endorsing the Great Replacement theory, which holds that Democrats are using illegal immigration to replace the current electorate and cement power, Vance wrote on social media , “Tucker Carlson is the only powerful figure who consistently challenges elite dogma—on both cultural and economic questions

Don’t fall for it this time, or any other.” Vance went on to endorse the same theory in advance of the next midterm elections. “Democrat politicians who have decided that they can’t win reelection in 2022 unless they bring in a large number of new voters to replace the voters that are already here” are orchestrating lax border enforcement, he said on Carlson’s show that year
The Carlson-Vance partnership has generated more conservative blowback over the past few years as Carlson has progressed from skepticism of Israel into anti-Semitism , which Carlson denies

Traditional Republicans who have supported, or at least gone along with, the party’s attacks on Muslims and immigrants and its rejection of democratic norms have spoken out against cracking the door open for anti-Semites

Building an authoritarian, ultranationalist party that marinates in populist conspiracy theories but that abhors anti-Semitism turns out to be tricky. [ Helen Lewis: Carlson and Vance—two smart guys who play dumb for power ] Vance, heading into his expected 2028 presidential campaign, has a strong incentive to try to harness this right-wing energy
His political interests would be served if Republicans were to stop attacking Carlson and if Carlson were to tone down his criticism of the GOP
Hence, he seemed less concerned that Carlson had crossed a moral line than that, in the Michigan Senate race, he had crossed party lines
Carlson praising a member of the Democratic Party is more threatening to Vance than Carlson praising an apologist for the National Socialist German Workers’ Party

At this week’s press conference, the reporter asked Vance, “What do you say to those who are uneasy with your close relationship with Carlson and claim that you’re avoiding addressing a lot of these issues, which may be causing divisions within the GOP?” “What a travesty it is that in the United States of America, we let political disagreements define who our friends are going to be and not going to be,” Vance said. “So, yeah, Tucker is a friend of mine.” Suppose Carlson decided to support someone other than Vance for president in 2028
Does anybody think their friendship would survive?

title: The Rush-Job Presidency
excerpt: Construction is notoriously slow-going work
body: Construction is notoriously slow-going work
But in Donald Trump’s Washington, cranes and bulldozers appear like DoorDash deliveries: fast, frictionless, and on demand
To build the president’s White House ballroom, roughly 250 workers have been pouring concrete and installing steel framework, keeping the site humming for 20 hours a day, seven days a week

The National Park Service has proposed a similarly intensive schedule for Trump’s planned triumphal arch: Construction will begin, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced on Thursday, in the next two weeks
And officials are trying to shut down the Kennedy Center for two years to carry out renovations that consultants say will take twice as long if the building remains open during the work
These are very different and ambitious projects, but they share the same presumed deadline: January 20, 2029
They also share a risk: The compressed schedules could lead to shoddy work that will require more repairs later
Trump has less than three years to complete his transformation of Washington, D.C., before his projects fall into—and perhaps die in—the hands of a successor. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone
When I leave here, nobody will,” he told New York magazine
The next president, whomever they are, likely won’t share Trump’s enthusiasm for gold finishes and Italian marble
To get the work done, his administration has found ways to circumvent the procedural obstacles that tend to slow federal projects
Construction—one of the world’s least productive industries—may present its own paradox
Research has shown that long hours, additional shifts, and overlapping work tasks can shorten a project’s timeline—but only to a point
In many cases, the effort to build faster can invite new delays, higher costs, and revisions
Trump’s botched repairs to the Reflecting Pool ahead of the nation’s 250th-birthday celebrations, in July, offer a classic example of the problem
The ballroom project, a hulking party venue that overshadows the White House’s main building and its modest neoclassical design, could be another
The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 this week that its construction could continue, saying that the preservationists trying to halt the project did not have standing to sue
The three liberal dissenting justices—along with, notably, Chief Justice John G
Roberts—argued that the construction was “likely unlawful.” But government filings claim that it’s already 65 percent complete—even as project leaders have continually revised design plans

By the time a new lawsuit from a challenger with stronger standing advances through the courts, how far along will the ballroom be? [ Read: The Court’s ballroom decision is a sign of deeper problems ] “We have hundreds of happy construction workers in D.C. busily doing their job building the finest Ballroom/Military complex anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social this week after the Supreme Court decision
With his lawyers saying that the project will be “substantially” finished by November, the clock is ticking fast
Trump’s building spree presents a tricky calculation: The returns he wants are about time rather than cost
But speed in construction can get expensive fast, especially for a project whose anticipated costs have been hard to nail down
When Trump announced the ballroom plans in July 2025, he put the price at roughly $200 million, to be paid for by private donors
By October, he’d knocked down the East Wing of the White House without seeking any approvals

As the work has started, stopped (because of the preservationists’ lawsuit), and started again, the original estimate has tripled to $600 million, and taxpayers are expected to cover half of that amount, according to internal documents from the ballroom’s general contractor, Clark Construction, that were obtained by The Washington Post

Those projections could rise again. “Accelerated construction is always at higher cost, no matter what you do,” Awad Hanna, the chair of the construction-engineering and -management program at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, told me

There are essentially three ways to make construction move faster, according to Hanna: Workers can put in overtime, contractors can add second or third shifts, or the project can resort to overmanning—that is, adding an unusually large number of workers to a site
Each method may buy some time but sacrifices some productivity, Hanna said
Researchers have documented that trade-off for decades

A 1997 study published by the American Society of Civil Engineers examined 121 weeks of labor-productivity data from four industrial projects and found efficiency losses of roughly 10 to 15 percent for 50-to-60-hour workweeks
Hanna’s own research has found similar patterns
With overmanning, the problem is that there’s only so much room for specific tasks to be performed
As the site fills up with workers, they can find themselves competing for tools, materials, and information—or simply getting in one another’s way
Meanwhile, overtime can lead to fatigue for workers who are spending 10 to 12 hours on their feet, carrying heavy objects while also needing to remain diligent about their own safety
There is another way to speed up construction without adding hours or workers: starting construction before a design is complete

But a 2023 study found that construction professionals perceived the fast-track strategy as posing a different set of risks, including construction errors and productivity declines, when better productivity is supposed to be the whole point
A certain amount of secrecy surrounds the White House worksite, in part because of a large military structure that is being built underground, beneath where the ballroom will stand

The methods to speed up the work are unclear, although the teams behind the project are reputable: Clark Construction is a seasoned federal contractor, and the architectural firm Shalom Baranes Associates repaired the Pentagon after 9/11
A White House spokesperson told me that the project is proceeding with the 20-hour schedule for now

title: Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth
excerpt: Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college
body: Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college

New research from Stanford shows that, even though the much-hyped AI job apocalypse has yet to materialize, the technology has already caused a nearly 20 percent drop in employment for young workers in AI-exposed occupations, such as computer programming and customer-service work
Anxiety over the looming threat of AI may seem novel, but as a cognitive scientist who has long studied how fear affects learning and performance, I am all too familiar with this kind of unease
Several years ago, my former graduate student Ian Lyons and I invited people who were anxious about math to have their brains scanned while they took a math test
We were surprised to find that it wasn’t the test itself that sent people’s brains into a panic

Rather, the neural signals associated with threat detection and pain were most acute when people were merely anticipating the test. [ John Paul Rollert: A society of cheats ] We are all now living through AI’s waiting-for-the-math-test phase
AI is transforming classrooms, workplaces, and hiring needs—and experts say more turbulence is coming
Teachers and students are struggling to parse the difference between deploying AI effectively and exploiting the technology to cheat
But rather than tackling this disruptive change and the resulting anxiety head-on, many educators are trying to make AI simply go away
The University of Chicago’s social-science faculty have prohibited most technology and banned the use of AI tools from their core classes
Although law firms are beginning to embrace the benefits of generative AI, the technology apparently makes many law schools squeamish

In May, the UC Berkeley School of Law announced that students are prohibited from using AI in “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.” The University of Chicago Law School has decided to ban all screens from first-year classrooms entirely
In an atmosphere of uncertainty—and given prevailing concerns about students using AI to cheat—such bans would seem to make some sense
But draconian mandates and screenless classes can’t be the only ways that colleges deal with AI
If universities hope to remain relevant in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, they should strive to guide students to understand and use these tools productively
In my research of math anxiety, we found that the best cure was practicing math

When we supply students with the space to thoughtfully explore and engage with these tools, we can help ensure that they graduate into an AI-enabled workforce with more confidence and competence than fear, and with an appreciation for how to use AI tools ethically

But if higher education opts for prohibition over practice, we will squander the chance to help shape how this technology gets used in the world—ensuring that the private sector will do this for us instead
Colleges must start by being clear about what a degree is actually worth in the AI age

At Dartmouth, the Ivy League university where I am president, we believe it’s our job to teach students how to do what AI can’t: decide which questions to ask, exercise sound judgment, navigate ethical complexity, reckon with uncertainty, and take responsibility for their decisions
Then, we have to give them the chance to practice these skills in concert with AI
Harnessing AI ethically and productively requires understanding what the technology is and where it falls short

This is why Dartmouth, along with other schools such as Johns Hopkins University and Rollins College, has employed a critical AI librarian , an educator who helps students and faculty interrogate these models, recognize their biases, and spot unsupported claims
At our DALI Lab , where students design and create technological products, they can now build and stress-test their own AI models, which elevates their understanding of the risks and rewards at play
Our ambition at Dartmouth is for every undergraduate to experience a team-based AI project that relates to their coursework by the time they graduate
Practice using AI matters even more when students start to specialize

To help prepare business students for AI use in the real world, Dartmouth’s Tuck School of Business now requires that they use the technology to build and test solutions for clients in their First-Year Project
Thanks to this experience, students who lacked AI expertise when they entered the program reported greater confidence using the technology by the end of their first year

At Dartmouth’s Geisel School of Medicine, our faculty developed an AI Patient Actor to help medical-school students sharpen their communication and interpersonal skills with the benefit of real-time feedback

The tool is now being used by more than 100 medical institutions worldwide. [ Walt Hunter: Bring back the blue-book exam ] Adapting the college experience for the AI era will be an ongoing process, and there is much work to do
But these examples demonstrate what’s both possible and necessary in higher education
Our job as educators is to teach students how to approach AI critically, help them see what AI can’t answer, and practice using these tools effectively
When these students graduate and are out in the world, employers will certainly expect that they have these skills already
Globally, jobs that require advanced AI skills are growing eight times faster than the job market overall, according to an analysis from the professional-services network PwC

At the same time, entry-level roles in AI-exposed fields are more than seven times likelier than other entry-level jobs to require the human skills once reserved for senior executives, including discernment, creativity, and leadership
Never before has the ability to harmonize critical thinking and technology mattered more for graduates
There will not—and should not—be a one-size-fits-all solution to the challenges of supplying this education
One professor may decide that students should write their essays in a blue book in class, while another may ask them to use an AI tool and audit every step of this work
Both choices will serve students when faculty are clear about their ambitions and standards
But outright bans or vague curbs afford no opportunities for students to better understand how to work ethically and effectively with AI

title: Gen Z’s politics aren’t what people think
excerpt: An attendee during a debate watch party with the Miami-Dade Young Democrats in Miami, Florida, on September 10, 2024. | Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty
body: An attendee during a debate watch party with the Miami-Dade Young Democrats in Miami, Florida, on September 10, 2024. | Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images After 12 years of dominating American politics — either as president, as a candidate, or from the sidelines — Donald Trump will finally exit the stage in 2028, and it’s anybody’s guess what will come next
But one thing we do know is that Gen Z, many of whom were children during Trump’s first campaign, will play a large role in shaping that future
What’s less clear is what direction they might choose or what their politics are in the first place
We do know a few things, thanks to a Vox collaboration with the polling firm Murmuration
For one, they’re highly independent: Almost 30 percent answered “none of the above” when they were asked to choose their political label in Murmuration’s survey
They’re an economically insecure cohort, at least for now; Murmuration found that only 28 percent of respondents between the ages of 18 and 30 said they could cover an unexpected expense of $500
And they had the largest gender gap of any age group when it came to supporting the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 — women preferred Kamala Harris by 17 percentage points over men
To find out more, Vox’s Astead Herndon spoke with Gen Z researcher Rachel Janfaza for a recent episode of America, Actually
They discussed the group’s political identities, preferences, and top issues, and what that all could mean for politics going forward
They discussed an important distinction between two versions of Gen Z, and whether its infamous gender gap is shifting
They also touched on how, contrary to seemingly everyone else, Gen Z is hope-maxxing
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Janfaza, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
You’ve done a lot of work around the different Gen Zs
I’ve heard you talk about Gen Z 1 versus Gen Z 2
How would we describe those differences? I call this the theory of the two Gen Zs

I really started to cultivate it doing focus groups with young people in 2022, hearing the way that high school students at the time and college students at the time just had a different outlook, and I realized that those who had graduated high school before the start of the pandemic, those Gen Z-ers, just had a different worldview than the younger half of Gen Z, who were still in high school at the time that the pandemic hit
And that is because of the taste of independence that people on the older cusp of Gen Z had prior to the lockdown situation
Anyone who is between roughly 29 and 22, I would say, is Gen Z 1.0, and anyone younger than that would be Gen Z 2.0
And there’s no official end date to Gen Z right now
Like, it’s sort of 1997 to 2012, so it’s not very clear yet
Can you just name for me what the difference was between the generations? How did that shape a different form of politics? Gen Z 1.0 really came of age during Trump’s first term in office
He was breaking down past barriers, and we saw a lot of youth-led activism in response to actions or inaction from the first Trump administration
You saw things like the March for Our Lives and climate strikes and the Black Lives Matter movement
And there was this very real sense that, you know, if we protest and demand change, perhaps there could be a difference
Whereas Gen Z 2.0 came of age during the Biden era

And they really grew resistant to authority because they saw Democrats in charge during the time when kids went back to school and when there were things like mask mandates and vaccine mandates, especially in blue areas across the country where Democrats were handling the way that schools were reopening
Young people whose lives and childhoods were on the line felt like they were guinea pigs in an experiment that they didn’t sign up for, and I think this is when we saw a movement away from Democrats
I don’t necessarily think that was toward Republicans
Broadly speaking, Gen Z 2.0 is far less trusting of authority and institutions, far more independent
They hate labels, and this isn’t just political
They hate labels when it comes to gender, their relationships
I hear this all the time in my focus groups, and so they just moved away from both parties writ large
I also want to ask a couple of questions specifically about the gender divide, because that was such a big topic in the 2024 election
We heard at that time, and I reported on, the change among young men that we saw manifested in that race
There was a 17-point gap between the votes of Gen Z men and Gen Z women
Before we get to where we are now, what do you think drove that gap? No
The easy thing to say is it’s the algorithm, but that’s not the whole picture
I think a lot of young women felt like their bodily autonomy, freedom, rights were on the line
And a lot of young men care about that, but when I asked them, “What’s the top issue in the 2024 election?” few said abortion

title: How to survive a national debt scare
excerpt: An electronic billboard on a bus stop in Washington, DC, displays the current US national debt on August 30, 2026. | Jemal Countess/Getty Images for the Peter G
body: An electronic billboard on a bus stop in Washington, DC, displays the current US national debt on August 30, 2026. | Jemal Countess/Getty Images for the Peter G
Peterson Foundation The national debt hasn’t been a major issue in the 2026 midterms
As of last month, the United States is in debt to the tune of $40 trillion

That’s 12 zeros, which averages out to about $116,000 per American.  It’s enough that even economists like Jared Bernstein, the chair of the US Council of Economic Advisers under President Joe Biden, is starting to worry

Bernstein has long argued that the national debt is nothing to worry about too seriously as long as servicing it — that is, paying the interest on it — remains manageable.  Bernstein has since changed his tune

He told Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram after last month’s debt milestone that while the number itself is “a big distraction,” two factors have him worried: Congress’s inaction and rising interest rates
But is it well and truly time to panic? Are we in a moment of no return?  Below is an excerpt of Sean’s conversation with Bernstein, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Have you now or ever been wrong about the national debt? Yes
Who hasn’t? Tell me what your position was and why you think it maybe was wrong
A lot of the economic work on the national debt involves forecasting, predicting where things are going

And nobody can really forecast things like interest rates or when there’s going to be another recession or a war or a pandemic, so nobody could honestly answer that question with, “I’ve been right about everything.” But I feel good in the sense of being intellectually honest about how I’ve thought about this
When the numbers were pointing to a level of calmness about our fiscal outlook, even though lots of people had their hair on fire, I didn’t go there

I was pretty adamant that there wasn’t anything to be overly worried about at this point, for reasons that we can get into.  When the numbers changed, and the outlook changed, and the politics changed, I changed
Let’s start with why you thought it was okay to carry loads of debt in the first place, because that was your position for some time, right? Correct
When you say loads of debt, the important thing is not just this load of debt or the stock of debt
Think of the debt as the water in the bathtub and think of the flow
Every year, you get a deficit or a surplus

That’s the water coming into the bathtub.  If you have a large stock of debt or loads of debt, as you say, which we were carrying, what you really want to look at is: What’s the rate of interest? How much debt service do you have to pay to your creditors on that stock of debt? And as long as the interest rate stays pretty low and the country’s ability to service its debt is manageable, there’s no obvious reason to break out a sweat, even if there’s a lot of water in the bathtub.  As long as you’re growing faster than your interest rate payments, as long as you’re not adding too much to the debt every year, underlying economic growth can allow you to service that debt without breaking a big economic sweat
And that’s where we were for a bunch of years
Would you say you were part of an economic consensus in this country? I would say yes, with an asterisk that maybe it was 50-50

Half of us who were watching it had hair that wasn’t burning up and the others had smoke coming out of their hats.  By the way, there’s an interesting strain here that we shouldn’t miss because it becomes more and more relevant over time
Of the hair-on-fire group, there were two classes

One was genuinely freaked out, incorrectly in my view, and the other was a bunch of politicians who pretended to have their hair on fire, but really didn’t.  “Don’t get hung up on the big, round number
It’s just not okay if your debt grows faster than your economy.” These were — I used to call them chicken hawks
They were budget hawks, but they didn’t really want to do anything about it
And in fact, they consistently pushed in the wrong direction, which turned out to be kind of an important component of my apotheosis in this space
Something happens at some point during this Trump administration that changes your mind
It wasn’t like at 2:37 pm on a particular day, just to be clear

I saw a number of things eroding and it wasn’t just during the Trump administration.  Something flipped in my head a little bit because any kind of what we call a reaction function by Congress, to react to these unsustainable forecasts, looked dead to me
And then I started seeing some academic work that actually measured this and showed, lo and behold, Congress was no longer reacting to the budget outlook
That was part one.  Part two is I started to see interest rates drift up

And if you’ll recall earlier, as I think you put it, interest rates found their way into the conversation.  [Part three], we saw budget deficits that in normal times — the budget deficit, which again, that’s the water flowing into the tub — should be negative 2 to 3 percent
That’s almost a recessionary-level deficit
So you put those three things together and my head broke

Do you think this congressional inaction or indifference to the debt was somehow seeded by decades of economists like yourself, saying, “This is okay”? Let me flip that on you, because I don’t want to hold myself or my colleagues unaccountable, but I actually think the other side may be even more to blame or equally to blame in the sense of, they were saying the economy is about to explode for 30 years
And it didn’t.  Now it is true that those of us — speaking for myself, I was saying, “We really ought to get our fiscal house in order, but we don’t need to worry about an immediate crisis
We have time to fix this.” I was trying to be nuanced, but American politics doesn’t do nuance, so you can blame me for that
We still have time to fix this and the sooner we start, the better.  When I talk about debt unsustainability and the potential for a debt spiral, I’m talking about over the next decade
The good news, Sean, is that there are ways to start repairing the damage

title: Architecting memory and storage in the AI era
excerpt: Imagine a healthcare system analyzing millions of data points in real time to accelerate life-saving medical research, or an intelligent assistant instantly res
body: Imagine a healthcare system analyzing millions of data points in real time to accelerate life-saving medical research, or an intelligent assistant instantly resolving thousands of complex customer needs at once

These real-world breakthroughs rely on advanced infrastructure acting as the engine of continuous intelligence, powering real-time services while also supporting an increasingly intelligent edge of IoT and consumer devices
However, in this inference-driven landscape, every delay, bottleneck, or wasted watt directly affects human outcomes and operating costs.  This shift changes what infrastructure must deliver
Performance, latency, memory bandwidth, storage throughput, and networking cannot be optimized in silos

Inference workloads are continuous, geographically distributed, and highly sensitive to response time, requiring systems designed for scale, resilience, and efficiency from the start. “We tend to think of AI as a single workload, and it’s not
It’s thousands, it’s millions, it’s billions of different workloads,” says Jim McGregor, founder and principal analyst, Tirias Research
AI inference changes the optimization problem from one of raw compute to coordinated infrastructure—memory, storage, and networking
For business leaders, the priority is clear: AI infrastructure decisions must balance cost, flexibility, and future readiness
The winners will be organizations that improve performance per watt, reduce environmental footprint, and remove memory and storage bottlenecks before they limit growth
AI inference requires a new architectural approach Systems for AI need to be rearchitected because shoehorning modern AI systems into legacy infrastructure limits AI’s transformative potential
Purpose-built architectures are essential to realize the true value of AI, from accelerating scientific discovery to creating truly autonomous digital agents

Traditional enterprise IT has been able to rely on relatively stable infrastructure assumptions, but inference and agentic AI introduce new demands around latency, data movement, scalability, and utilization that make architecture choices far more consequential. “Data centers must now support continuous, distributed, and increasingly real-time AI services—none of which are a single workload,” says McGregor. “They all require different requirements from a system-level perspective.” To support real-time AI, enterprises can no longer view memory and storage merely as supporting hardware, but at the heart of the system
Organizations need to architect a data pipeline that can rapidly ingest, clean, transform, store, move, and deliver data

Inference workloads place sustained pressure on infrastructure in ways that look very different from earlier training-centric deployments, demanding continuous data retrieval and caching that traditional applications never required
Accordingly, performance by itself is no longer the sole benchmark that matters

Enterprises increasingly must balance performance with efficiency, cost, and scalability, especially as they try to support different AI services without overbuilding infrastructure for peak conditions. “You have to optimize the entire network, and that includes memory and storage, around the types of workloads you plan on running,” says McGregor. “You have to really have a detailed understanding of what those workloads are going to be.” Any AI infrastructure strategy must start with workload awareness
Inference, agentic AI, and other emerging AI use cases require organizations to treat the data center as an integrated system

Data movement is the new bottleneck and an opportunity for competitive advantage As enterprises deploy advanced inference and agentic systems, the sheer volume of data being queried in real time has made data movement the most pressing constraint
Modern AI techniques like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) require systems to constantly scan massive databases to generate accurate responses
This requires immense computing power, but more importantly, it requires immediate access to data

McGregor says the focus shift to how efficiently data can be moved, cached, and delivered across the broader architecture elevates memory and storage from background infrastructure to strategic assets. “The biggest thing we’re doing right now is moving data from one place to another and making sure that we can use it effectively.” Because AI is not a single workload category, simply buying the fastest processors is insufficient
Inference depends heavily on memory bandwidth, caching, storage proximity, and the ability to retrieve relevant information quickly and consistently
Understanding where each resource belongs in the stack and how those layers interact under real operating conditions has become a business imperative

The most effective AI infrastructure looks less like a collection of best-in-class parts and more like a balanced system of compute, memory, storage, and networking, McGregor says, because bottlenecks tend to migrate from one layer to the next. “You have to architect all four together to be efficient, and that’s the challenge.” The interdependence of data-plane design and network bandwidth means AI infrastructure planning has become a business decision just as much as an engineering one: latency is now inseparable from value
In robotics, financial services, healthcare, and customer-facing AI systems, delays are not merely technical imperfections; they can undermine safety, responsiveness, or trust
AI infrastructure performance becomes a matter of reputation management

The organizations that gain the most from AI may not be those with the largest clusters, but those with the clearest understanding of how to align every infrastructure element to effectively execute AI workloads
Building an AI infrastructure procurement framework Planning AI infrastructure is not simply about choosing the fastest hardware

It is about how to scale without locking the organization into assumptions that may quickly become obsolete. “You need to be flexible because the demands are going to change rapidly and the technology is changing rapidly,” McGregor says
Future-proofing AI infrastructure requires keeping your options open as workloads, economics, and architectures keep shifting: Define the AI workloads that are being optimized
Infrastructure choices must match business needs rather than what McGregor calls generic “AI readiness,” which risks overspending in some areas while leaving bottlenecks unresolved in others
Build a modular architecture for compute, memory, storage, power, and cooling so capacity can change as demand shifts rather than committing too early to a rigid architecture
Work with the full ecosystem of suppliers and integrators to reduce supply risk and improve access to the right components
McGregor says buyers can no longer assume their OEM or cloud provider alone will insulate them from supply constraints or architectural complexity
Reassess your procurement strategy continuously
AI requirements, hardware, and business models are changing too quickly for a fixed long-term design
Optimize for efficiency and ROI, not just peak performance
The most powerful setup may be too costly to sustain
Efficiency is also a public-facing metric—better utilization and more workload-aware system design can help companies respond to growing scrutiny around power consumption and water use
The strategic goal of smarter AI data center design is not maximum performance at any cost, but an adaptable architecture that can deliver value, absorb change, and justify its footprint

title: Data from drones in Ukraine is fueling a new Wild West marketplace
excerpt: Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones, which are now firmly established as a critical weapon of modern warfare
body: Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones, which are now firmly established as a critical weapon of modern warfare
But behind all that wreckage, there’s a new gold mine for the defense sector

The data drones generate will far outlast the wars in which they are used to fight, increasingly becoming part of the AI architecture that shapes even civilian life.   For every flight, unmanned systems collect thousands of points of data, from images and video to controller inputs
Together, those records show how a machine and a person responded to constantly shifting circumstances.  Ukraine has now begun converting that experience into a resource

Its Ministry of Defense announced in January that it would make millions of data points gathered during tens of thousands of drone flights available to both military contractors and commercial companies, and since then more than 100 companies and the UK government have gained access
For a country at war, it’s a quick way to attract funding and partnerships
But this step turns the front line into an active site of model training, taking advantage of how the chaos of war creates conditions that AI companies struggle to reproduce on their own
Other countries and battlefields are likely to follow Ukraine’s lead, but the responsibility for governing this new industry cannot fall solely on a country fighting for its survival

That legal vacuum has to be filled together by the countries and companies involved in this industry’s development.   Explosive growth Ukraine’s battlefields are not the first to produce records used to train and develop models: American drones over Syria and Yemen collected data that informed the first generation of semiautonomous military hardware in the late 2010s
The difference now is that access to that data is being used to develop a wider ecosystem
And the financial value to defense firms is immense: Battlefield data offers large volumes of machine experience gathered under conditions that no laboratory can produce
That’s because the data that’s most valuable for training AI models comes from exceptions: the moment visibility disappears, a signal jams, or a human operator improvises
AI companies spend years and enormous sums trying to capture enough of these moments to make their models more robust
But war produces them at a frequency controlled testing cannot match
This constantly changing terrain is what makes drone data valuable far beyond the battlefield
A commercial drone used for delivery or remote sensing may never encounter artillery fire, but it must still operate with incomplete information in a world where people behave unpredictably
The same problem is compressed by war into a much shorter timeline.  Processed and matched against records of what its operator was doing, that data turns operational records into training sets
Many conflicts have already seen this training loop happen as drone footage feeds subsequent generations of military technology, and the market is set to grow

Enabled Intelligence, an American company that specializes in processing data to become usable in AI training, says it has already made more than half a million hours of Ukrainian drone footage available to feed into the next round of models, advertising possible uses in both military and commercial systems
Closing the data loop Many of the drones that now define our modern age of warfare began as civilian technology

But they’ve recently been turbocharged by new, commercially available AI systems, which allow cheap machines to operate autonomously—either individually or as a flock—as the environment changes around them
Each flight then creates a record of what the system encountered
The controlled lab environments usually developed to train these autonomous systems can approximate failure but are no match for  the live conditions of a battlefield with very real risks

Military intelligence programs have held data generated by sensor-heavy systems like Predator and Reaper drones for nearly a decade through programs like Project Maven, but access remained entirely within the defense world

The data generated was available only through restricted, classified channels for the sole purpose of developing new weapons systems that would feed back into the same military that produced the data in the first place
That experience is now being shared to a much broader development network.  The loop now closes

Commercial technologies adapted for the battlefield are generating data that can flow back into the industries from which they came, becoming part of the data infrastructure relied on by governments and the private sector alike.  Drones that were trained in the signal-jammed airspace over Ukraine are now being deployed in the agricultural sector to help farmers map and survey their fields in places lacking the cell signal necessary for previous generations of technology.  Other countries are likely to follow Ukraine in selling their battlefield data, and we are not ready for the new marketplace this will create
Bad actors could acquire the data, but purchase controls already mitigate that risk
Intelligence operatives scrutinize potential customers’ infrastructure for ways that data could reach enemies or nefarious actors.  Training data creates a new tracing problem, though

Whereas the movement of commercial datasets can be followed when planted contact details appear two steps from the original buyer, the provenance of AI training data vanishes in a manner embedded in the technology itself

Another risk is that this use of the data creates an extractive economy in which wealthier countries far from danger benefit from the mortal threat borne by frontline states, potentially creating a market incentive for war to continue as an unending mine for digital gold.  A fraught new frontier Existing laws regulate how militaries may conduct war

But they say almost nothing about what happens when records created in combat are stripped of their operational context, packaged as data, and licensed to companies whose products circulate far beyond where they were made
The responsibilities of the companies that design these systems remain unsettled

Ukraine is building access controls, which are mentioned in the newly signed UK-Ukraine AI agreement, but no governments are actively working on regulating what happens when data has been absorbed into a model and crosses back into civilian markets
The soldiers and civilians visible in them did not agree to become training material for products that might be sold years later
But sensor data, camera footage, and coordinates from civilians fleeing a drone strike now constitute the sorts of data that inform how future machines will make decisions
Individuals featured in the data—be they targets, controllers, or civilians standing by—become part of the training material
The autonomous capabilities based on that data do not stop at the edge of the battlefield
Such capabilities move into other military or commercial systems like delivery vehicles or agricultural machinery
Errors and assumptions embedded in the data travel with the model even once it enters civilian life

title: What comes next for the 1 million people who have lost – or will soon lose – Temporary Protected Status
url:
<title>What comes next for the 1 million people who have lost – or will soon lose – Temporary Protected Status</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757614/original/file-20260902-50-v9o6m3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6797%2C4531&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People hold Haitian flags and signs during a July 2026 rally in San Diego in support of immigrants living in the U.S. with Temporary Protected Status.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Immigration%20TPS/139c819321fb441096bf602bdafda502/photo">AP Photo/Gregory Bull</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>At the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, <a href="https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/fact-sheet/temporary-protected-status-tps-overview/">1.3 million individuals from 17 countries</a> were living and working in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status, or TPS.</p>

<p>TPS is a humanitarian form of protection from deportation for people who cannot return to their home countries because of an armed conflict, environmental disaster or other <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1254a">extraordinary circumstances</a>. </p>

<p>In 2025, the Trump administration began terminating or not renewing TPS for those countries, making its way through 13 of them. As the administration turns its attention to the few remaining nations, most TPS holders have lost or will soon lose their protection from deportation and their authorization to work. Many will be separated from their families and the communities <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/12/second-trump-administration-has-ended-temporary-protected-status-for-most-immigrants-who-had-it/">they have lived in for decades</a>. Some will be forced to return to countries like Afghanistan, Haiti and Syria, all of which are on the U.S. State Department’s <a href="https://travelmaps.state.gov/TSGMap/">“Do Not Travel” list</a> due to war, terrorism or other extreme violence. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://gould.usc.edu/faculty/profile/jean-lantz-reisz/">law scholar</a> who studies immigration detention, I can say that most people with TPS never had a path to anything more permanent, which means, as they face deportation, they have little recourse. </p>

<h2>Challenges in court</h2>

<p>In the fall of 2025, the Trump White House announced that it would not renew Syrian or Haitian TPS; Syria’s would expire in 60 days, Haiti’s in February 2026. Lower courts blocked both terminations, triggering appeals that took the cases to the Supreme Court.</p>

<p>In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-1083_f204.pdf">the Supreme Court ruled</a> that federal courts cannot review most challenges to a TPS termination because, in <a href="https://guides.loc.gov/latinx-civil-rights/tps">the original 1990 law creating TPS</a>, Congress barred judicial review of the decision to give a country TPS – or extend or end it.</p>

<p>James Percival, the general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, <a href="https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/06/25/dhs-issues-statement-following-multiple-supreme-court-wins">celebrated the decision</a>, saying “Temporary Protected Status was always supposed to be temporary and can be canceled at the appropriate time.”</p>

<p>But the ruling means no court can consider whether a cancellation is, in fact, “appropriate,” or whether it follows the law. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

<h2>Unanswered questions</h2>

<p>When Congress passed TPS as part of <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/101st-congress/senate-bill/358">the Immigration Act of 1990</a>, it was responding to a specific failure: the ad hoc and inconsistent use of something called Extended Voluntary Departure, which permitted a noncitizen to remain in the U.S. <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/25/25-1083/404231/20260413110419518_MiotCongress_Amici%20Document%20%20%20%20%20April%2013%202026%20EFile.pdf">regardless of their immigration status</a>. </p>

<p>That discretionary relief allowed some displaced Salvadorans to remain in the U.S. during their country’s civil war in the 1980s, but its application was arbitrary and often <a href="https://ccrjustice.org/home/what-we-do/our-cases/american-baptist-churches-v-thornburgh">discriminatory</a>. Because the <a href="https://americanarchive.org/exhibits/newshour-cold-war/el-salvador">U.S. backed the Salvadoran government</a>, Salvadorans were denied both Extended Voluntary Departure and asylum <a href="https://www.migrationpolicy.org/journal/country-profile/el-salvador-despite-end-civil-war-emigration-continues">more than 90% of the time</a> – not for lack of merit but because of the government they were fleeing.   </p>

<p>Congress recognized a humanitarian need for more uniform protection for people who, like Salvadorans, faced a return to violence or extreme danger but were not covered by narrow asylum laws that require proof of targeted persecution. </p>

<p>A new protected status would “standardize the procedure for granting temporary stays of deportation,” <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/25/25-1083/404231/20260413110419518_MiotCongress_Amici%20Document%20%20%20%20%20April%2013%202026%20EFile.pdf">Representative Sander Levin explained</a> at the time.</p>

<p>“Refugees, spawned by the sad and tragic forces of warfare, should not be subject to the vagaries of our domestic politics as well,” Levin added. When the 1990 Immigration Act passed, El Salvador was the first country designated for TPS.</p>

<p>Congress avoided placing time limits on these new TPS designations, leaving that to the discretion of the presidential administration, which would evaluate a country’s humanitarian needs <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS20844">at least every 18 months</a>. Whether TPS holders should ever gain something more permanent was left for future congressional action.</p>

<h2>No next step</h2>

<p>Not every person from a TPS-designated country is eligible for it. Anything that disqualifies someone from asylum – national security concerns, persecuting others or criminal history – also <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/temporary-protected-status">disqualifies them from TPS</a>. </p>

<p>Congress did not want to incentivize unlawful immigration. For that reason, it wrote the law in such a way that TPS itself could not lead to permanent residence. Lawful permanent residents are eligible to become citizens <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/citizenship/learn-about-citizenship/citizenship-and-naturalization/i-am-a-lawful-permanent-resident-of-5-years">after five years</a>. TPS recipients, though living in the U.S. lawfully, are not classified as lawful permanent residents. </p>

<p>Congress has since passed laws creating a pathway to permanent residence for certain nationalities, including some with TPS – the <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/refugees-and-asylum/asylum/nicaraguan-adjustment-and-central-american-relief-act-nacara-203-eligibility-to-apply-with-uscis">Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act</a>, for example. It did not do so for most.</p>

<p>TPS designations for some countries have ended after a few years, like Rwanda and Guinea; others have been renewed for decades, like El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua. Over the years, TPS became a kind of limbo status, dependent on each presidential administration’s regular evaluation of a country’s humanitarian conditions – and on Congress to turn TPS into a pathway to lawful permanent residence. For most, the latter never happened. </p>

<h2>What happens when TPS ends?</h2>

<p>Many people who lose TPS are not eligible for any other immigration status. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.uscis.gov/green-card/green-card-processes-and-procedures/adjustment-of-status">Lawful permanent residence</a>, commonly known as a “green card,” is mainly available in three ways: through a close family relationship, like being married to a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident; through a job that requires special skills, like being a professional soccer player; or through asylum status. </p>

<p>Even if a person can apply for permanent residence, their immigration history, such as entering the U.S. without a visa or remaining in the U.S. without lawful status for a certain time, <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/cases/sanchez-v-mayorkas/">may be a permanent barrier</a>. </p>

<p>TPS holders are given at least <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1254a">60 days’ notice</a> before termination takes effect, at which point they lose authorization to work and become undocumented, meaning they can be arrested by immigration officers at any time. There is little they can do in those 60 days that would allow them to lawfully remain in the U.S.</p>

<p>A TPS holder who has been continuously present in the U.S. for more than two years has a right to an immigration hearing before removal, where they may be able to apply for asylum or other relief. Others may hope to switch to a different status, but most TPS holders cannot obtain a student or employment visa. Some would have to apply from outside the U.S., some face years of quota backlogs, and some are from countries under a travel ban.</p>

<p>Past immigration violations or insufficient financial resources would also disqualify them. Most significantly, TPS holders are unlikely to convince an immigration officer that they intend to return home after their visa’s purpose is complete, as most visas require – especially someone from a country in distress due to violence or environmental disaster, the reason they have TPS in the first place. </p>

<p>Some <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/12/second-trump-administration-has-ended-temporary-protected-status-for-most-immigrants-who-had-it/">300,000 people</a> from El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine and Lebanon are set to lose status this year. <a href="https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/international-travel/International-Travel-Country-Information-Pages/Ukraine.html">Ukraine</a> and <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/06/middleeast/americans-lebanon-homes-destroyed-israel-latam-intl">Lebanon</a> are in active war, so terminating TPS means deporting those people to war zones, which is what TPS was meant to prevent. Some TPS holders from El Salvador and Sudan have lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years. </p>

<p>Perhaps the 1990 Congress did not anticipate that individuals with TPS would make the U.S. their home for so long. Whatever it envisioned, it did not limit TPS to a fixed time. In my analysis, Percival’s assertion that TPS was always meant to be temporary is not, by itself, an “appropriate” reason to end protection. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-1083_f204.pdf">Justice Elena Kagan stated in her dissent</a> to the recent Supreme Court ruling, even if TPS does not promise “never-ending humanitarian protection,” the end of it for certain individuals – like the plaintiffs in Mullin v. Doe – could deliver them to “devastating, and indeed life-threatening, injury.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290292/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Farmer-poet Wendell Berry’s environmental ethics were deeply rooted in his Christian faith and belief in caring for creation</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757904/original/file-20260903-50-9xbk1d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C66%2C4332%2C2888&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Wendell Berry, right, joins an &#39;I Love Mountains&#39; rally against mountaintop mining at the Kentucky Capitol in 2013. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/KY%20Mountaintop%20Removal/244ed389603d4cb6a684afa6402885f0/photo">AP Photo/James Crisp</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For most of his 92 years, Wendell Berry farmed his Lane’s Landing homestead in Henry County, Kentucky, using <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america/">methods that embraced the land</a>. He preferred draft horses to diesel-powered tractors and used crop rotation and manure fertilizer to naturally nurture his fields.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://religionnews.com/2026/09/01/wendell-berry-writer-and-farmer-extolled-by-many-as-a-modern-day-prophet-dies-at-92/">widely revered</a> poet-farmer, who wrote passionately about rural American life and humans’ responsibility to care for the land, believed in practicing what he preached.</p>

<p>Those beliefs were rooted firmly in <a href="https://www.christianitytoday.com/2026/09/wendell-berry-obituary-novelist-poet-christian-agriculture/">his Christian Baptist faith</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/95VcefsgsfE?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Wendell Berry interviewed by Bill Moyers. The Berry Center.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Throughout his life, Berry, who died on Aug. 31, 2026, was a leading <a href="https://www.loa.org/books/606-what-i-stand-on-the-collected-essays-of-wendell-berry-1969-2017-boxed-set/">advocate of environmental stewardship</a>. You might recognize his belief system in what’s known as <a href="https://biologos.org/common-questions/why-should-christians-care-for-creation">creation care</a> today. </p>

<p>It embraces a responsibility to care for the Earth and all its creatures. Berry increasingly saw that ethic violated by the industrialization of agriculture and ignored by a <a href="https://www.christiancentury.org/article/features/quiet-rise-christian-dominionism">dominionist theology</a>, preached by some prominent American Christians, which holds that humans have a God-given right to exploit the Earth’s resources.</p>

<h2>Biblical base for Berry’s environmental ethics</h2>

<p>Berry’s environmental ethics had their basis in Genesis, the first book of the Bible, which emphasizes that humans are not the owners of the Earth but rather are called to be caregivers and to tend the planet. He wrote, “We are allowed to make no exceptions – every person’s obligation toward creation is <a href="https://www.christiancentury.org/article/2004-11/hymn-creation">summed up in two words from Genesis 2:15</a>: ‘Keep it.’” </p>

<p>In contrast, the <a href="https://www.christiancentury.org/article/features/quiet-rise-christian-dominionism">dominionist view emphasizes</a> Genesis 1:8, which has been interpreted by some to mean that humans are to subdue the Earth and to establish Christian dominance. </p>

<p>Berry opposed the idea that Christian scripture advocated for environmentally destructive practices such as mountaintop-removal coal mining, which led to the destruction of streams and forests in his native Kentucky. In 2011, he participated in a multiday sit-in protest of the mining practices, saying, “I <a href="https://sojo.net/articles/wendell-berry-wont-quit-trying-save-mountains">intend to stay interested in it and involved</a> as long as the Lord spares me.” </p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An image from a social media site" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

          </figure>

<p>I am a <a href="https://history.uiowa.edu/people/kristy-nabhan-warren">scholar of American Christianity</a> and have spent my career researching and writing about how Christians practice their beliefs. I was in the audience when Berry was awarded the 2013 American Academy of Religion’s <a href="https://aarweb.org/award/martin-e-marty-award-for-the-public-understanding-of-religion/">Martin Marty honor for the Public Understanding of Religion</a>. For over an hour I listened raptly, as did the rest of the standing-room-only crowd, as he detailed his love for the land, community and his wife, Tanya.</p>

<p>I also taught students using his book “<a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/jayber-crow/">Jayber Crow</a>,” about small-town living, religion and community, in my honors course at a small liberal arts college in the Midwest. I returned to his work when I was researching modern-day agriculture in Iowa for my book “<a href="https://uncpress.org/9781469663494/meatpacking-america/">Meatpacking America</a>”.  </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">

<p>I saw how Berry’s beliefs that humans have a responsibility to care for the Earth shaped his critiques about “agripower,” which he viewed as <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america-50th-anniversary-edition/">showing little regard for the fertility of the soil</a> or the “health, wisdom, thrift, or stewardship of the farming community.” His poems, fiction and nonfiction often <a href="https://www.loa.org/books/606-what-i-stand-on-the-collected-essays-of-wendell-berry-1969-2017-boxed-set/">advocated for consuming less and living more communally</a>.</p>

<p>Those beliefs rested on his <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america/">commitment to caring for God’s creation</a>.</p>

<h2>The idea of ‘enough’</h2>

<p>Berry’s <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-long-legged-house/">Christianity-infused agrarianism</a> began in earnest in the 1970s and helped popularize family-run farms, organic farming and farm-to-table eating establishments.</p>

<p>The modern creation care movement began as part of a wider network of American social justice movements. It took shape in the 1980s and ’90s, especially <a href="https://denverseminary.edu/2023/06/13/evangelicals-and-creation-care/">among those Christian evangelicals</a> who read the Book of Genesis as instructing humans to care about all of God’s creations. Today, creation care is a <a href="https://oikoumene.org/news/christians-are-called-to-care-for-creation">broad Christian movement</a> that calls for environmental stewardship, repairing the harm that humans have done to the environment, and belief in a loving God who is responsible for the Earth’s creation.</p>

<p>As the religious studies scholar <a href="https://users.drew.edu/lkearns/about.html">Laurel Kerns</a> has written, the Christian environmental movement that began in the 1980s laid the theological groundwork for creation care. Today’s many chapters of creation care form <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/3712004">part of a religious environmental movement</a> that calls for Christians to embrace stewardship, creation spirituality and ecojustice. </p>

<p>As he detailed his 1977 text “<a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america-50th-anniversary-edition/">The Unsettling of America</a>,” Berry was a fierce critic of agribusiness and <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/667717/why-i-am-not-going-to-buy-a-computer-by-wendell-berry/">American’s throwaway, consumeristic culture</a>. He admired the Amish lifestyle, which forgoes modern conveniences for simple farm living focused on God and family. He wrote, “It is possible, I think, to say that this is a Christian agriculture, formed upon the understanding that it is sinful for people to misuse or destroy what they did not make. The Creation is a unique, irreplaceable gift, therefore <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america-50th-anniversary-edition/">to be used with humility, respect, and skill</a>.”</p>



<p>Berry encouraged people, whether or not they identified as Christian or as religious, to question technology as the Amish do, to consider its impact on the environment as well as on human lives, and to develop the concept of “enough.” He wanted people to be more intentional and reflective in their thoughts, words and actions.</p>

<p>Throughout his poems and other writing, Berry beseeched readers to focus on what they actually need and not what they want or think they need. “The <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/standing-by-words/">idea of ‘enough’</a> is alien to capitalism, which respects no limit,” he wrote.</p>

<h2>Wendell Berry’s legacy in an AI backlash</h2>

<p>Berry and his wife and collaborator for 69 years, <a href="https://www.kentuckypress.com/author/tanya-amyx-berry/">Tanya Amyx Berry</a>, built a way of life and advocated for a way of living that went against the grain of mainstream American and global culture.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/wendell-berry">over 50 books and many poems</a> and talks, Berry helped lay the theological, ethical and how-to groundwork for a creation care movement that spread around the world. He consistently called out the extractive, destructive human behaviors that have posed dangers for the planet’s future.</p>

<p>How his legacy will be fulfilled remains to be seen, but if the growing cross-generational <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-local-communities-are-challenging-big-tech-data-centers-noise-pollution-and-rising-electricity-bills-284642">public aversion to AI data centers</a> and other forms of resource extraction are an indicator, it is my belief that Wendell Berry’s legacy will have a long and fruitful afterlife.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291025/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
