<title>Mosquitoes are picky eaters – we studied 3 common South Florida species to learn why they like some people more than others</title>
    <content type="html"><p>If you’ve ever had to prepare a meal for a picky eater, you know it’s not easy. They may not like certain flavors or textures, and there are often foods you have to avoid altogether.</p>

<p>And it turns out, humans aren’t the only species with picky eaters – mosquitoes can also be finicky.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/kaylee-marrero-552819218">We are</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=HW-XRN4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">biology researchers</a> who study mosquito behavior, and we recently discovered that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117006">mosquitoes can be picky about their favorite food</a> – that is, human blood.</p>

<p>Learning what attracts these mosquitoes could be useful to <a href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-best-mosquito-repellents-according-to-science/">designing repellents that deter them</a> from biting people and reducing the local populations of mosquitoes that spread disease. And understanding why the living community of microbes on our skin appeals to mosquitoes could help in the development of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae267">probiotic mosquito repellents</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1200%2C1200&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="illustration showing three different types of mosquitoes flying around a group of people" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1200%2C1200&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755773/original/file-20260824-50-k26gre.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Alejandro Acuna</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Meet the mosquitoes</h2>

<p>Our study focused on three mosquito species: <em><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/aedes-aegypti">Aedes aegypti</a></em>, <em><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/aedes-albopictus">Aedes albopictus</a></em> and <em><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/culex-quinquefasciatus">Culex quinquefasciatus</a>.</em> All three are abundant where we live in South Florida, among many other places.</p>

<p>Of course, the average person won’t be able to tell which species of mosquito bit them, especially since they might not realize they’re being bitten in the moment. But we looked at each of these species, since they pose different health risks to humans.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/aedes-aegypti"><em>Aedes aegypti</em></a> live in urban environments, primarily in warm climates, and they prefer biting humans over animals. They are responsible for spreading diseases to humans like the <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/16077-zika-virus">Zika virus</a>, which can cause birth defects, and <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/dengue-fever/symptoms-causes/syc-20353078">dengue fever</a>, which can cause a rash, vomiting and, in severe cases, hemorrhaging and dangerous drops in blood pressure.</p>

<p><em><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/aedes-albopictus">Aedes albopictus</a></em>, also known as the Asian tiger mosquito, are an invasive species in the U.S. They love biting humans, but these mosquitoes will venture out of urban environments in search of a good meal. They also spread dengue fever, as well as <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/25083-chikungunya">chikungunya</a>, which causes fever and joint pain. </p>

<p>The final mosquito species, <em><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/culex-quinquefasciatus">Culex quinquefasciatus</a>,</em> prefers to find a bite to eat in suburban areas in southern U.S. states. For these mosquitoes, also known as the southern house mosquito, their favorite meals are birds – but they also bite humans. This makes them an integral component of the bird-human disease cycle, spreading illnesses like <a href="https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and-diseases/west-nile-virus">West Nile virus</a>, which can affect the nervous system and, in severe cases, lead to death.</p>

<h2>No humans were bitten during this study</h2>

<p>We recruited 119 participants and tested their attraction for each species using a device called a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1101/pdb.prot108174">uniport olfactometer</a>. It’s an acrylic container made up of three parts – a box where the human participant could place their arm, a tube into which we released the mosquitoes, and a smaller tube, called the attraction chamber, connecting them. A mesh screen divides the chamber from the participant’s arm so that the mosquitoes could get up close but couldn’t bite the participants.</p>

<p>We classified mosquitoes that traveled down the tube and into the attraction chamber as attracted to the participant. There is a funnel on the inside of the attraction chamber, so once the mosquitoes entered, it was difficult for them to go back. We calculated the rate of attraction for each participant by counting how many mosquitoes entered the attraction chamber.</p>

<p>For each participant, we released 30 mosquitoes at a time into the olfactometer. We tested each species three times, for a total of 90 mosquitoes tested per species and 270 mosquitoes per participant. We observed that each of the three species had their own preferences for which humans they wanted to bite.</p>

<p>Every person’s skin has <a href="https://theconversation.com/skin-mouth-lungs-its-not-just-your-gut-that-has-a-microbiome-208516">its own unique microbiome</a> – a community of microorganisms that live on the skin and keep it healthy. Typically, this includes <a href="https://dermnetnz.org/topics/microorganisms-found-on-the-skin">a combination of bacteria species</a> such as <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK8448/"><em>Staphylococcus</em></a>, <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/corynebacterium"><em>Corynebacterium</em></a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/microorganisms9020303"><em>Cutibacterium</em></a>.</p>

<p>Both the amounts and combinations of these microbes can change, depending on a person’s diet or overall health. In order to ensure the best possible sample from each person’s skin, we asked our study participants not to wear any perfumes or deodorants and to refrain from showering or bathing for at least 12 hours prior to coming into the lab.</p>

<p>Our team collected skin odors from each of the participants by having them put their arm inside a bag immediately after the attraction trials. Their arm was also swabbed for microbes so we could identify which bacterial species were present. This allowed our team to determine which odors and microbes each mosquito species was looking for.</p>

<h2>What mosquitoes did – and didn’t – like</h2>

<p>Each species showed clear preferences when it came to the odors and skin bacteria. </p>

<p><em>Aedes aegypti</em> showed a slight preference for men over women, while the other two mosquito species did not discriminate on the basis of sex. The reasons for this are not clear, and the differences in odors and skin microbes between men and women were too great for us to tease out any individual factors driving mosquito attraction. </p>

<p><em>Aedes aegypti</em> preferred people that had less of certain odors like <a href="https://molekula.com/index.php/product/isomenthol">cyclic alcohols</a>, which are ingredients in some fragrances and cosmetic products. But they were attracted to people on whom <em>Staphylococcus</em> bacteria was more abundant. Meanwhile, lower attraction was associated with certain <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/25164-pseudomonas-infection"><em>Pseudomonas</em> bacteria</a>. </p>

<p><em>Aedes albopictus</em> was a little less picky, preferring people with plenty of odors. They particularly sought out people with high amounts of organic compounds called <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/ketone">ketones</a>. One of their favorite ketones was <a href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Mesityl-oxide#section=Chemical-Classes">mesityl oxide</a>, which has a sweet, honeylike odor. These mosquitoes also preferred people with more skin microbes, particularly when bacteria like <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/17460913.2024.2423524"><em>Streptococcus intermedius</em></a> and <a href="https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(26)00175-0"><em>Anaercoccus octavius</em></a> were in higher abundance.</p>

<p>But they also avoided certain bacteria, like the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1099/00207713-52-1-115"><em>Mogibacterium</em> genus</a>. We suspect that these bacteria may produce odors that these mosquitoes don’t like.</p>

<p>Much like <em>Aedes aegypti</em>, <em>Culex quinquefasciatus</em> picked participants that had fewer odors overall. They were attracted to <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms21197078">monoterpenes</a> like <a href="https://abstraxtech.com/blogs/learn/alpha-pinene-health-benefits">alpha-pinene</a>, which are organic compounds often found in essential oils.</p>

<p>Interestingly, there were no bacteria that were associated with high attraction for <em>Culex quinquefasciatus</em>, but there was a high abundance of the bacteria <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/24981-actinomycosis">genus <em>Actinomyces</em></a> on the participants that were low attraction to these mosquitoes.</p>

<p>The results weren’t all differences: Some odors and bacteria were attractive across all three species. For example, all three were attracted to participants with the <a href="https://shop.perfumersapprentice.com/p-6075-ethyl-methyl-2-butyrate.aspx">odor chemical ethyl 2-methylbutanoate</a>, a fruity scent often found in fragrances. And all three species were less attracted to participants with lots of the <a href="https://www.thegoodscentscompany.com/data/rw1027961.html">odor 1-penten-3-ol</a>, a chemical typically used in fresh- or crisp-scented products.</p>

<p>We also found that some skin bacteria were attractive across all three species. For example, people with more <a href="https://doi.org/10.1128/spectrum.03578-22"><em>Corynebacterium kefirresidentii</em></a> living on their skin were highly attractive to all the mosquitoes.</p>

<h2>No person was attractive to all mosquito species</h2>

<p>Scientists have known <a href="https://www.conncoll.edu/media/website-media/images/content/chemistry/illuminatingdiseasepdfs/mos-attraction.pdf">for decades</a> that <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-are-some-people-mosquito-magnets-and-others-unbothered-a-medical-entomologist-points-to-metabolism-body-odor-and-mindset-187957">some people are more attractive to mosquitoes</a> than others, and they have been studying these mosquito magnets since the 1960s.</p>

<p>We therefore expected that a few of our 119 participants would be mosquito magnets, and that these people would attract all three species. So we were surprised to find that no human was a universal mosquito magnet among these three species. The enticing aromas that allow each mosquito species to find us are just too different. </p>

<p>This tells us that mosquitoes can act as picky foodies with their own preferences for people and how they smell. Looking at the skin bacteria that help to make humans smell, there are clear differences and commonalities in terms of what attracts these mosquitoes. body: If you’ve ever had to prepare a meal for a picky eater, you know it’s not easy
They may not like certain flavors or textures, and there are often foods you have to avoid altogether
And it turns out, humans aren’t the only species with picky eaters – mosquitoes can also be finicky
We are biology researchers who study mosquito behavior, and we recently discovered that mosquitoes can be picky about their favorite food – that is, human blood
Learning what attracts these mosquitoes could be useful to designing repellents that deter them from biting people and reducing the local populations of mosquitoes that spread disease
And understanding why the living community of microbes on our skin appeals to mosquitoes could help in the development of probiotic mosquito repellents
This study looked at which mosquito species are attracted to which people, and why
Alejandro Acuna , CC BY Meet the mosquitoes Our study focused on three mosquito species: Aedes aegypti , Aedes albopictus and Culex quinquefasciatus
All three are abundant where we live in South Florida, among many other places
Of course, the average person won’t be able to tell which species of mosquito bit them, especially since they might not realize they’re being bitten in the moment
But we looked at each of these species, since they pose different health risks to humans
Aedes aegypti live in urban environments, primarily in warm climates, and they prefer biting humans over animals

They are responsible for spreading diseases to humans like the Zika virus , which can cause birth defects, and dengue fever , which can cause a rash, vomiting and, in severe cases, hemorrhaging and dangerous drops in blood pressure
Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito, are an invasive species in the U.S
They love biting humans, but these mosquitoes will venture out of urban environments in search of a good meal
They also spread dengue fever, as well as chikungunya , which causes fever and joint pain
The final mosquito species, Culex quinquefasciatus , prefers to find a bite to eat in suburban areas in southern U.S. states
For these mosquitoes, also known as the southern house mosquito, their favorite meals are birds – but they also bite humans
This makes them an integral component of the bird-human disease cycle, spreading illnesses like West Nile virus , which can affect the nervous system and, in severe cases, lead to death
No humans were bitten during this study We recruited 119 participants and tested their attraction for each species using a device called a uniport olfactometer

It’s an acrylic container made up of three parts – a box where the human participant could place their arm, a tube into which we released the mosquitoes, and a smaller tube, called the attraction chamber, connecting them
A mesh screen divides the chamber from the participant’s arm so that the mosquitoes could get up close but couldn’t bite the participants
We classified mosquitoes that traveled down the tube and into the attraction chamber as attracted to the participant
There is a funnel on the inside of the attraction chamber, so once the mosquitoes entered, it was difficult for them to go back
We calculated the rate of attraction for each participant by counting how many mosquitoes entered the attraction chamber
For each participant, we released 30 mosquitoes at a time into the olfactometer
We tested each species three times, for a total of 90 mosquitoes tested per species and 270 mosquitoes per participant
We observed that each of the three species had their own preferences for which humans they wanted to bite
Every person’s skin has its own unique microbiome – a community of microorganisms that live on the skin and keep it healthy
Typically, this includes a combination of bacteria species such as Staphylococcus , Corynebacterium and Cutibacterium
Both the amounts and combinations of these microbes can change, depending on a person’s diet or overall health

In order to ensure the best possible sample from each person’s skin, we asked our study participants not to wear any perfumes or deodorants and to refrain from showering or bathing for at least 12 hours prior to coming into the lab
Our team collected skin odors from each of the participants by having them put their arm inside a bag immediately after the attraction trials
Their arm was also swabbed for microbes so we could identify which bacterial species were present
This allowed our team to determine which odors and microbes each mosquito species was looking for

<title>Essential digital technologies are critical infrastructure – they are not always built and managed that way</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757351/original/file-20260901-50-1x9xow.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5472%2C3648&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Passengers fill a terminal at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas on July 19, 2024, after a major internet outage disrupted flights worldwide.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Worldwide-Internet-Outage-Airlines/6662c96973b4495883583c788cdb5756/photo">AP Photo/Ty ONeil</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>What do the water system in Flint, Michigan, the electrical grid in Puerto Rico and your search engine have in common? They are all critical infrastructure – systems essential to everyday life.</p>

<p>People expect critical infrastructure to be reliable, to minimize risk and to promote public well-being. When it fails – such as when lead seepage <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6309965/">poisoned Flint’s water supply</a> in 2014, or when nearly all of <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/12/31/nx-s1-5243984/puerto-rico-power-outage-blackout-new-years-eve">Puerto Rico’s power went out</a> on New Year’s Eve in 2024 – the public expects risks to be mitigated and problems to be addressed.</p>

<p>Today’s <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/topics/critical-infrastructure-security-and-resilience/critical-infrastructure-sectors">critical infrastructure</a> includes food and water systems, roads and bridges, and financial and health systems. Much of the digital technology everyone depends on is also critical infrastructure. People depend on search engines for information, social media for public announcements and important communications, and AI-powered services for analysis and decision-making. All are essential to function in modern civic society. </p>

<p>When search engines opportunistically <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691244006/algorithms-for-the-people?srsltid=AfmBOooBy07AwUNjxgICufltHi-UfMrQXkZ3PEi-n1xllU40B_sy3t58">shape the information that people seek</a>, social media is <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417419307043">polluted with misinformation</a>, and AI-driven services serve up <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cpd8l088x2xo">unsafe recommendations</a> or “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/17/technology/ai-slop.html">digital slop</a>,” many people chalk it up to the <a href="https://innovation.consumerreports.org/new-report-mapping-the-accountability-gap-in-ai-powered-financial-services/">cost of engaging with the commercial sector</a> and feel <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/10/18/how-americans-view-data-privacy/">powerless to control their information</a> – or one form of “<a href="https://theconversation.com/protecting-privacy-online-begins-with-tackling-digital-resignation-198979">digital resignation</a>.”</p>

<p>My experience as former director of the <a href="https://www.sdsc.edu">San Diego Supercomputer Center</a> and co-founder of the international <a href="https://www.rd-alliance.org">Research Data Alliance</a> suggests that it doesn’t have to be this way. Digital infrastructure can be designed, built and managed for human well-being just as other critical infrastructure is. </p>

<p>To do so, society will need to change both its expectations about digital critical infrastructure and its actions – the way the public and private sectors create and regulate these services and systems and the way the public uses them – to better protect the people who depend on them. </p>

<h2>From food to search engines</h2>

<p>People expect critical infrastructure to be safe and secure for widespread use. They expect it to be broadly accessible and reliable, and to promote public interests at least as much as commercial profit. This means incorporating safeguards for the public such as speed limits on roads, redundant systems in power plants, and privacy regulations governing health data. It is never perfect, but people expect critical infrastructure to be built, managed and regulated to support and protect a vulnerable public.</p>

<p>Consider food and <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/topics/critical-infrastructure-security-and-resilience/critical-infrastructure-sectors/information-technology-sector">information systems</a>: Both sustain the well-being of the public in different ways. In <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/topics/critical-infrastructure-security-and-resilience/critical-infrastructure-sectors/food-and-agriculture-sector">the food system</a>, public <a href="https://www.nal.usda.gov/human-nutrition-and-food-safety/food-safety-standards">health standards</a> safeguard the way your food is processed so that it does not make you sick. Restaurants are evaluated based on their compliance with these health standards: Is food handled and stored at safe temperatures? Are kitchens sanitized properly? In many places, restaurants must publicly display the letter grade the health department gives them. It’s easier to make healthy choices when you know if a restaurant got an A or a C.  </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/xROaKfmo9fE?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Social media has become critical infrastructure, too.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Search engines are also critical infrastructure, shaping how people access information essential to modern life. Yet the ranking systems of opportunistic search algorithms often prioritize content that is commercially advantageous, heavily optimized and attention-grabbing. These priorities shape public understanding, influence democratic discourse and can sometimes give users a distorted view of reality. </p>

<p>What if people expected search engines to provide similar transparency about how they select and rank content? What if you knew a search engine’s algorithmic priorities, how it profiles you as a user and how advertising shapes the information you receive? That might help you decide where to look for information and how much to trust what you find.</p>

<p>Digital critical infrastructure can put people at risk in different ways. Sometimes people feel the impact immediately, as when the power grid blacks out or the internet goes down. Sometimes it fails by exposing people to a toxic environment – a polluted river can harm the people and wildlife that depend on it, just as dangerous misinformation on social media promoting <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/27/well/facebook-supplements-health.html">health scams</a> or <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10471190/">body dysmorphia</a> can harm people seeking information and advice. Sometimes digital critical infrastructure fails by not including sufficient protections – by creating a fertile environment for <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/15/nyregion/social-media-scam-sextortion.html">predators</a> or by supporting <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/01/ftc-surveillance-pricing-study-indicates-wide-range-personal-data-used-set-individualized-consumer">surveillance pricing</a> models that use personal information to extract the most that consumers can pay.</p>

<p>To counteract these risks, it’s important to incorporate more safeguards in the design, deployment and management of the systems people depend on. It’s also important to provide users with more control over what they see on social media and who appears in their feeds, and more transparency about how the personal data collected by connected doorbells or e-commerce services is used, shared or sold. Such safeguards could reduce risk and help users avoid exploitation, manipulation and predators.</p>

<h2>Where to start?</h2>

<p>Making digital critical infrastructure better is within reach, and the strategies described in my book, <a href="https://www.franberman.com">Better Tech:  Putting <em>People</em> First in Cyberspace</a>, and elsewhere can make tech both better, and better for the people who depend on it. </p>

<p>Consider transportation as an example. Experts predict that self-driving cars will be <a href="https://www.vtpi.org/avip.pdf">ubiquitous in the coming decades</a>. Engineers can reduce tomorrow’s public risks today by designing these connected <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/MM.2022.3219803">“data centers on wheels” to reduce emissions</a> from onboard computers, protect passenger data and create fail-safe measures needed to operate safely when the internet on tomorrow’s connected highways goes down. Such efforts involve human planning, work and intervention now to ensure that future transportation will promote public well-being.</p>

<p>Digital critical infrastructure can be built and managed better; people’s well-being depends on it. The challenge today is to ensure that as we develop the technologies that shape our future, they also advance society and help humans thrive.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288580/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Francine Berman is a Trustee of the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, former Director of the San Diego Supercomputer Center, and co-founder of the Research Data Alliance.  </span></em></p></content>

Johnson</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/">CC BY-NC-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The case against social media has gotten so well rehearsed that most people can easily merge it into ordinary conversation: It makes people lonely. It sorts them into camps. It hands them a room full of people who already agree with them and calls that a community. </p>

<p>I’ve given this speech myself, with feeling, having read my phone notifications in the host’s powder room 11 minutes earlier. </p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://ldi.upenn.edu/fellows/fellows-directory/kevin-b-johnson-md-ms/">pediatrician, health communicator and researcher</a> at the University of Pennsylvania, and diagnosing is in my blood. <a href="https://www.nationalacademies.org/projects/HMD-BPH-21-14/publication/27396">Two decades of research</a>, a <a href="https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf">surgeon general’s advisory on loneliness</a> and <a href="https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-secures-171-billion-and-groundbreaking-reforms-meta">Meta’s recent settlement of up to US$17 billion</a>, pending court approval, all describe the same thing. What we recite are the symptoms. The more interesting question is what these symptoms diagnose.</p>

<p>Simply put, our dependency on social media creates a deficiency disease. It’s not something toxic we’re ingesting; it is something our lives online have stopped us from receiving.  </p>

<p>I figured out that cost while standing in a field in Harford Park with a dog leash wrapped around my ankles.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<h2>A corner bar without the alcohol</h2>

<p>Harford Park in Wayne, Pennsylvania, is 30 acres of rolling grass and mature trees the township <a href="https://www.radnor.com/Home/Components/FacilityDirectory/FacilityDirectory/22/33">designated for off-leash dogs in 1997</a>. </p>

<p>I go most afternoons. So do the same 15 or 20 people, which is how I ended up tangled in someone else’s very long leash on a Tuesday, concentrating hard enough on my own feet that I stopped talking and just listened.</p>

<p>Two conversations were running at once. In one, a regular who is having a rough year was getting gently harassed about the weight he’d put on against his doctors’ advice — first by me, then by three other people who piled on uninvited. In the other, someone was arguing about Dr. Anthony Fauci, and the regulars chimed in on both sides. Gossip, complaints and dogs greeting dogs became the backdrop.</p>

<p>As I worked to free my ankles, it clicked: The dog park, like the local knitting club or the Saturday pickleball group, does the job a corner bar used to do. There are regulars and running jokes, and once a person is known, a spot in the conversation is reserved for them.</p>

<p>What makes these places work is that a shared focus on one small part of a life opens into something fuller. Regulars may share a taste in dog breeds or beer, but they are not colleagues, political soulmates or relatives. They differ on favorite restaurants, income, age, religion, values and beliefs. They are together because a golden retriever and a nervous rescue mutt need to run in the morning, and there is a field nearby.</p>

<h2>Chance encounters can increase empathy</h2>

<p>Sociologist Ray Oldenburg called places like this <a href="https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/ray-oldenburg-phd/the-great-good-place/9780786752416/">third places</a> and defined them as “public places that host the regular, voluntary, informal, and happily anticipated gatherings of individuals beyond the realms of home and work.” Oldenburg noted the erosion of places that once manufactured accidental encounters, such as main streets, neighborhood pubs, general stores and even the drugstore soda fountain.</p>

<p>Off-leash parks have been <a href="https://www.tpl.org/media-room/dog-parks-lead-growth-us-city-parks">among the fastest-growing amenities in U.S. city park systems</a> for two decades. A study in the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07352166.2017.1343634">Journal of Urban Affairs</a> found dog park users reported higher social capital and neighborhood cohesion.</p>

<p>The park is not a utopia. It’s a corner bar without the booze.</p>

<p>Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.90.5.751">meta-analysis of 515 studies</a> provides the best evidence for why these accidental connections matter. They found that contact between groups generally reduces prejudice, but the quality and circumstances of that contact matter. The more interesting finding came later, when they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.504">tested how it works</a>: The effect runs less through learning facts about the other group than through reduced anxiety, more empathy and more perspective.</p>

<p>That is exactly what the park does. The man I disagree with about nearly everything hasn’t changed his mind, and neither have I. What changed is that his politics is now maybe the eighth thing I know and appreciate about him, behind his dog’s bad hip, his sense of humor, the awful year he had and his love of what Philadelphians call “wooder ice.”</p>

<p>That shift, from opinions to a person, is why “just show people the other side” keeps failing online. When sociologist Christopher Bail and colleagues paid Republicans and Democrats to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1804840115">follow bots representing the views of the opposite party</a> on Twitter, the Republicans came out substantially more conservative than they went in. Democrats shifted slightly left, though not significantly. Exposure to opinions is not the same thing as exposure to a person. The feed gave people arguments. The corner bar gives people other people.</p>



<h2>Making room for tolerance and trust</h2>

<p>If <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/02750740251346805">the places people gather shape their health</a>, as a growing body of research suggests, then the shift from communities set by geography to communities assembled by algorithm creates a slow burn of intolerance and mistrust. </p>

<p>There are now <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0329466">decades of research on social media and anxiety</a>, and a growing body of experimental work about what algorithmic curation does to what people see. Almost none of it treats the encounter pattern as a health exposure.</p>

<p>Social platforms have mastered what German American sociologist Herbert Gans called <a href="https://doi.org/10.7312/gans17884">selective homogeneity</a>. They sort people by interests, identities, tastes and grievances, then make it easy to stay among people who feel familiar.</p>

<p>They are like virtual Levittowns – the postwar suburban developments outside Philadelphia, among other places in the Northeast, where thousands of identical houses went up on farmland and were sold to buyers screened by price. In early Levittowns, covenants <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780195314748.003.0002">barred Black families outright</a>.</p>

<p>In 1958, <a href="https://doi.org/10.7312/gans17884-014">Gans moved into a Levittown</a> in New Jersey and stayed two years doing research on its residents. He found that although original settlers and those who moved in by choice were happy, their rebellious teenage offspring, who had the fewest places to go and the least to do in those communities, were not. </p>

<p>This was an early, real-life sorting of the type that algorithms would make all too common 60 years later.</p>

<p>By contrast, repeated, low-stakes, in-person contact like the interactions between regulars at a dog park or corner bar creates room for tolerance and trust. People come back. They notice an absence. They share attention around a task, a place or a dog, rather than around presenting themselves or defending a position.</p>

<p>Deficiency diseases are easily treatable. Nothing has to be taken away; instead, something has to be given back.</p>

<title>Taxpayers don’t want to pay for new NFL stadiums – so why did politicians approve billions in subsidies to fund six new ones?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757850/original/file-20260903-50-uy8h3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5850%2C3900&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Beginning in 2027, the Tennessee Titans will play their home games in the new Nissan Stadium in Nashville. Over $1 billion in public dollars have been committed to the project.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/exterior-of-the-new-nissan-stadium-with-dome-being-built-news-photo/2236943712?adppopup=true">Wesley Hitt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When the Buffalo Bills play their 2026 season home opener <a href="https://www.democratandchronicle.com/story/sports/football/nfl/bills/2026/04/23/buffalo-bills-new-stadium-timeline-location-and-key-features/89752586007/">in the newly built Highmark Stadium</a>, it will mark the first game to take place at one of six new NFL venues scheduled to open over the next six seasons.</p>

<p>The Tennessee Titans will move <a href="https://nissanstadium.com/new-nissan-stadium/">into a new dome in 2027</a>. <a href="https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/48642772/browns-break-ground-24-billion-stadium-targeted-29">The Cleveland Browns’ stadium</a> is on track to be ready for the 2029 season, while the Washington Commanders are planning to <a href="https://www.hksinc.com/our-news/articles/hks-named-lead-architect-for-washington-commanders-new-world-class-stadium/">inaugurate their new stadium</a> the following year. <a href="https://www.chiefs.com/news/legacy-reimagined-kansas-city-chiefs-release-renderings-for-new-stadium-set-to-open-in-2031">The new homes for the Kansas City Chiefs</a> <a href="https://newstadium.denverbroncos.com/">and Denver Broncos</a> are scheduled to open in time for the 2031 season.  </p>

<p>When the Bills stadium was announced in 2022, economists called the US$850 million public contribution from New York and Erie County taxpayers <a href="https://theconversation.com/ive-studied-stadium-financing-for-over-two-decades-and-the-new-bills-stadium-is-one-of-the-worst-deals-for-taxpayers-ive-ever-seen-180475">a terrible deal</a>. </p>

<p>That public expense would soon be eclipsed by subsequent NFL stadium projects, with subsidies averaging more than $1 billion and totaling $5.74 billion for the venues whose budgets have been announced. The Chiefs, <a href="https://www.sportico.com/business/real-estate/2025/chiefs-kansas-stadium-cost-public-money-1234879708/">recipients of $1.8 billion from Kansas taxpayers</a>, lead the pack. Denver’s stadium costs are <a href="https://theconversation.com/broncos-say-their-new-stadium-will-be-privately-financed-but-private-often-still-means-hundreds-of-millions-in-public-resources-270053">not yet known</a>.</p>

<p><iframe id="cREvG" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/cREvG/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Horizontal column chart highlighting the billions of dollars in total costs for five future football stadiums, with each stadium's costs broken down by public contributions and private contributions."></iframe></p>

<p>Economists have been studying the public financing of stadiums and their escalating costs for decades, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/joes.12533">consistently finding</a> that the meager economic benefits to host communities simply don’t justify the massive public outlays they receive. </p>

<p>My recent book, “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197820247.001.0001">This One Will Be Different: False Promises and Fiscal Realities of Publicly Funded Stadiums</a>,” summarizes and explains the dour findings. Stadiums fail to generate economic growth because they mostly reallocate existing spending from elsewhere in the community, rather than stimulate new commerce. And any localized development and intangible benefits tend to be limited – nowhere near enough to justify the subsidies provided. </p>

<p>But I also consider another important question: If research demonstrates that sports venues are unwise public investments, why do state and local governments continue to subsidize them?</p>

<h2>New stadiums a no-brainer – for owners</h2>

<p>Even though many of today’s stadiums are in good enough shape to last for decades longer – the Green Bay Packers, for example, are about to play their 70th season at Lambeau Field – stadiums <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/pam.22534">tend to be replaced in 30-year cycles</a>. </p>

<p>This corresponds with typical lease lengths that teams sign with municipal landlords. When facility leases expire, teams often seize the opportunity to push for publicly funded improvements.</p>



<p>The NFL’s last building wave peaked around the turn of the millennium, so the current uptick in new venues is expected. This trend will likely continue over the next decade, as leases for the many venues that opened in the 2000s expire.  </p>

<p>Rather than sign a new lease for an existing stadium, team owners have every incentive to build newer, more costly structures. </p>

<p>For one, they benefit from the temporary surge in attendance and revenue that comes from opening a new venue. It’s a phenomenon that economists call the “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ecin.13231">novelty effect</a>” – as fans clamor to experience the modern amenities that new venues offer. Teams also directly benefit from moving their operations to upgraded state-of-the-art facilities.</p>

<p>But a public contribution doesn’t only reduce the owner’s cost of replacing a venue. It also promotes lavish spending. When a government partner is sharing the financial burden, teams tend to design more expensive structures, since owners bear only part of the cost but receive all the benefits. This results in the “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1527002514551803">gold-plating</a>” of facilities with extravagant features – like upgraded luxury suites, private clubs or a dome – that owners might not be willing to pay for on their own. </p>

<p>Though the Buffalo Bills’ Highmark Stadium may be the only new NFL stadium <a href="https://news.pollstar.com/2026/07/23/the-2-1-billion-bills-gambit-why-buffalo-said-no-to-a-roof/">without a dome</a>, its stacked design includes heated concourses and a specially designed snow-melting roof that covers a majority of seats. It also includes <a href="https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/bills-fans-heres-guide-highmark-070027611.html">three new exclusive clubs</a> for patrons who are willing to pay extra for added amenities, like climate-controlled spaces, field-level patio access, premium food and beverage options, and a private whiskey locker.   </p>

<h2>Waning public appetite</h2>

<p>When economists began <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/089124248800200306">scrutinizing stadium financing</a> in the 1980s, they concluded that the monopoly power of sports leagues was driving subsidies. </p>

<p>The thinking went that by restricting the total number of franchises, owners were generating greater public commitments by creating bidding wars among various municipalities. Elected officials were then forced to commit tax dollars to keep their hometown teams or risk losing them to another state or city and angering their voters.</p>

<p>However, that’s not exactly what has happened. </p>

<p>The NFL, the NBA, the NHL and MLB have each added between three and 11 new teams since 1990, which has reduced the number of relocation targets. Yet in that period, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/pam.22534">subsidies have only continued to grow</a>. </p>

<p>Many teams received new public facilities without threatening to move anywhere. And though relocation may have been mentioned as a possibility in public discussions, none of the NFL franchises slated to open new venues over the next five years dangled offers from competing markets as an implicit threat to move.</p>

<p>Furthermore, when the question of using tax dollars for stadium improvements is put on the ballot, voters have often opposed them. </p>

<p>The Chiefs’ initial request for public funds to renovate its current stadium was soundly defeated by a <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-chiefs-and-royals-couldnt-convince-kansas-city-voters-to-foot-the-bill-for-their-stadiums-227113">Jackson County referendum</a> in 2024. And surveys of voters <a href="https://vanderbilthustler.com/2023/04/25/vanderbilt-poll-finds-nashville-residents-pessimistic-of-citys-direction-disagree-with-state-legislature/">in Nashville</a> and <a href="https://sri.siena.edu/2022/04/25/while-nyers-strongly-support-new-bail-law-changes-only-1-3-think-they-will-decrease-crime-38-say-theyll-have-no-effect/">upstate New York</a> found that a majority opposed the Titans and Bills stadium deals.</p>

<h2>Politicians versus the people</h2>

<p>Public financing for stadiums doesn’t always fail at the ballot box. </p>

<p>Voters in <a href="https://www.okc.gov/News-articles/OKC-voters-approve-new-downtown-arena">Oklahoma City</a> and <a href="https://apnews.com/article/spurs-arena-vote-f4c2f4af74f348a741d80313bdf75543">San Antonio</a> recently approved new arenas for their NBA franchises.</p>

<p>But elected officials are far more likely to approve public subsidies. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/grow.12068">A recent review of public stadium votes</a> found that only 58% of referendums put before voters passed. When they did, the support was slim: just 51%, on average. </p>

<p>In contrast, 96% of the proposals considered by representative bodies were approved with 80% support.</p>

<p>Teams realize that cutting voters out of the decision-making process is the most effective way to obtain public financing.</p>

<p>After the Chiefs’ Arrowhead Stadium renovation proposal was rejected by voters in Kansas City, Missouri, the team turned to <a href="https://apnews.com/article/kansas-city-chiefs-stadium-3234d777c543a485f9d7326bcb7436ad">lawmakers one state over, in Kansas</a>, where the electorate wouldn’t have a direct say in its new stadium request. The Titans employed a <a href="https://tennesseelookout.com/2023/07/26/what-happens-when-a-cash-poor-billionaire-wants-a-new-sports-stadium-lobbying/">$1.6 million lobbying campaign</a> to help get subsidies approved by state and local representatives. The Bills similarly sought funding from its <a href="https://apnews.com/article/buffalo-bills-new-stadium-nfl-ae8acd789c51e1db1fa9c342d68d94fb">county and state legislatures</a>. </p>

<p>It’s no surprise that none of the new NFL venues were considered by referendums. In fact, only six of 39 public subsidy proposals for new stadiums that were considered between 2005 and 2017 <a href="https://doi.org/10.1123/jsm.2012-0210">were decided directly by voters</a>.</p>

<h2>The perks of office</h2>

<p>So why might a representative favor a project that the majority of their constituents oppose? </p>

<p>It’s difficult to get inside the minds of elected officials, but it likely helps that politicians tend to be <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2014/09/03/who-runs-for-office-a-profile-of-the-2/">male and educated</a> – a demographic that likes sports.</p>

<p>By supporting and promoting venue projects, elected decision-makers may personally benefit, while passing the costs to taxpayers. Wooing public officials with playoff tickets and luxury boxes <a href="https://wtop.com/virginia/2016/01/mcauliffe-defends-cabinet-members-free-redskins-ticket-as-part-of-push-for-new-stadium/">is a strategy</a> that teams have openly employed.</p>

<p>Government representatives often have access to exclusive events and premium spaces that sports venues offer. For example, New York officials have been <a href="https://nysfocus.com/2024/04/04/buffalo-bills-tickets-carl-heastie-hochul">criticized for attending Bills games</a> in a publicly subsidized luxury suite.</p>

<p>It’s understandable that stadium proposals may seem more persuasive when presented over cocktails in a private suite, sitting among other prominent citizens and surrounded by a buoyant crowd cheering on the hometown team. </p>

<p>Owners appear to have learned that even though they may not be able to fit a majority of the electorate into the owner’s box, there’s plenty of room for the municipal council.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290212/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Wesley Hitt/Getty Images When the Buffalo Bills play their 2026 season home opener in the newly built Highmark Stadium , it will mark the first game to take place at one of six new NFL venues scheduled to open over the next six seasons
The Tennessee Titans will move into a new dome in 2027
The Cleveland Browns’ stadium is on track to be ready for the 2029 season, while the Washington Commanders are planning to inaugurate their new stadium the following year
The new homes for the Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos are scheduled to open in time for the 2031 season
When the Bills stadium was announced in 2022, economists called the US$850 million public contribution from New York and Erie County taxpayers a terrible deal

That public expense would soon be eclipsed by subsequent NFL stadium projects, with subsidies averaging more than $1 billion and totaling $5.74 billion for the venues whose budgets have been announced
The Chiefs, recipients of $1.8 billion from Kansas taxpayers , lead the pack

Economists have been studying the public financing of stadiums and their escalating costs for decades, consistently finding that the meager economic benefits to host communities simply don’t justify the massive public outlays they receive
My recent book, “ This One Will Be Different: False Promises and Fiscal Realities of Publicly Funded Stadiums ,” summarizes and explains the dour findings
Stadiums fail to generate economic growth because they mostly reallocate existing spending from elsewhere in the community, rather than stimulate new commerce
And any localized development and intangible benefits tend to be limited – nowhere near enough to justify the subsidies provided

But I also consider another important question: If research demonstrates that sports venues are unwise public investments, why do state and local governments continue to subsidize them? New stadiums a no-brainer – for owners Even though many of today’s stadiums are in good enough shape to last for decades longer – the Green Bay Packers, for example, are about to play their 70th season at Lambeau Field – stadiums tend to be replaced in 30-year cycles
This corresponds with typical lease lengths that teams sign with municipal landlords
When facility leases expire, teams often seize the opportunity to push for publicly funded improvements
The NFL’s last building wave peaked around the turn of the millennium, so the current uptick in new venues is expected
This trend will likely continue over the next decade, as leases for the many venues that opened in the 2000s expire
Rather than sign a new lease for an existing stadium, team owners have every incentive to build newer, more costly structures
For one, they benefit from the temporary surge in attendance and revenue that comes from opening a new venue
It’s a phenomenon that economists call the “ novelty effect ” – as fans clamor to experience the modern amenities that new venues offer
Teams also directly benefit from moving their operations to upgraded state-of-the-art facilities
But a public contribution doesn’t only reduce the owner’s cost of replacing a venue
When a government partner is sharing the financial burden, teams tend to design more expensive structures, since owners bear only part of the cost but receive all the benefits
This results in the “ gold-plating ” of facilities with extravagant features – like upgraded luxury suites, private clubs or a dome – that owners might not be willing to pay for on their own

Though the Buffalo Bills’ Highmark Stadium may be the only new NFL stadium without a dome , its stacked design includes heated concourses and a specially designed snow-melting roof that covers a majority of seats

It also includes three new exclusive clubs for patrons who are willing to pay extra for added amenities, like climate-controlled spaces, field-level patio access, premium food and beverage options, and a private whiskey locker
Waning public appetite When economists began scrutinizing stadium financing in the 1980s, they concluded that the monopoly power of sports leagues was driving subsidies
The thinking went that by restricting the total number of franchises, owners were generating greater public commitments by creating bidding wars among various municipalities
Elected officials were then forced to commit tax dollars to keep their hometown teams or risk losing them to another state or city and angering their voters
However, that’s not exactly what has happened
The NFL, the NBA, the NHL and MLB have each added between three and 11 new teams since 1990, which has reduced the number of relocation targets
Yet in that period, subsidies have only continued to grow
Many teams received new public facilities without threatening to move anywhere

And though relocation may have been mentioned as a possibility in public discussions, none of the NFL franchises slated to open new venues over the next five years dangled offers from competing markets as an implicit threat to move
Furthermore, when the question of using tax dollars for stadium improvements is put on the ballot, voters have often opposed them
The Chiefs’ initial request for public funds to renovate its current stadium was soundly defeated by a Jackson County referendum in 2024
And surveys of voters in Nashville and upstate New York found that a majority opposed the Titans and Bills stadium deals
Politicians versus the people Public financing for stadiums doesn’t always fail at the ballot box
Voters in Oklahoma City and San Antonio recently approved new arenas for their NBA franchises

title: Can synthetic cells save the world?
excerpt: Associate professor Kate Adamala has been busy
body: Associate professor Kate Adamala has been busy

Her lab at the University of Minnesota takes chemicals and dead, isolated biological parts — like DNA, membranes, ribosomes — and puts them together into “synthetic” cells to see if they will come to life…or at least act alive
This summer, Adamala’s lab had a tremendous breakthrough
They made synthetic cells that can feed, grow, and divide

She decided to name them SpudCells, and says that they prove that one day building a fully living lab-made cell will be possible.  Adamala’s dream, and the dream of other synthetic biologists like her, is to make all the medicine, materials, and fuel we need with synthetic cells like these
Instead of relying endlessly on petrochemicals, Adamala believes we could program cells to generate these materials in a lab for a more self-reliant and renewable future
As Adamala explains: “I live in the Midwest, so we’ve got a lot of prairie grass
Why can’t I take that prairie grass and ferment it into a plastic toy? It’s totally possible
We just…don’t have a living organism that would be willing and able to do that.” The synthetic cell could eventually be that organism
Living cells can move atoms around with pinpoint precision without creating a lot of toxic waste along the way

The only problem is that natural biological cells are too hard to control.  Scientists still don’t actually understand how natural cells do everything they can do. “I’m scared of cells,” Adamala says. “I don’t believe that we’ll ever be able to understand a complex living cell
So my approach is I think we can build ourselves a cell.”   For Unexplainable ’s three-part Life From Scratch series, I spoke with some of the leading voices of synthetic cell biology

From making the world’s first living cell with synthetic DNA to racing to build safeguards against a technology that could kill the world , this series explores the potential promise and scary risks of synthetic cell biology
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Adamala about her lab’s big breakthrough, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast — and the whole series — so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and more
You can also watch a video version of this conversation on Netflix
What’s the big research that you shared with the public this summer?  We made a cell that can feed, grow, and divide out of nonliving, chemical components
People have been making cells from dead chemicals for a long time now, but none of them were able to realize those key functions of life
This is the first time synthetic cells have been able to grow and replicate based on their own instructions
Before, we could make a synthetic cell and tell it to grow by adding things to it, but the SpudCells grow because they feel like it, because the proteins inside them tell them to grow
So it can grow, it can eat, and it can divide
Are they alive? I don’t think they’re alive
Even though they do all those functions that we think only life does, they’re not doing any of it very well.  They have to be fed pretty much every building block that they need
Life needs to figure out how to survive, and the cells that we made, even if on the surface level they look like they fulfill the functions of life, there is no robustness in there
If the conditions are not absolutely perfect, they will just stop
This seems like it should be a simple question, but from our conversation, I get the sense that maybe it’s a little bit more complicated than it seems
What makes something alive?  That’s a very good question, and I think the best answer I can give is a quote from US Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart
He said, “I will know it when I see it.” It’s not a scientific definition, but there is no good scientific definition of life

There is a NASA definition of life that NASA has been using when they look for life in the universe, and that definition says “a self-replicating chemical system that’s capable of Darwinian evolution.” Okay.  And according to the NASA definition of life, you’re dead and I’m dead because I’m not self-replicating

So that just shows you that definitions of life are very inaccurate, very context-dependent.  There’s just not a good definition of life that would cover everything that we instinctively consider alive, and exclude everything that we would all agree is not alive
Everyone defines life according to some different principles
Why call these cells SpudCells?  We wanted to invoke Sputnik

It was the first artificial satellite, and it was actually a pretty bad satellite — it didn’t really do any of the things that fancy modern satellites do — but it basically opened up the Space Age.  It showed people that it’s possible to escape the gravity well
If we can put a satellite in orbit, maybe we can put people in orbit
And if we can put people in orbit, maybe we can escape orbit, go to the moon, and then go past the moon
And that’s how I see the role of a SpudCell
So it’s almost like a proof of concept?  Exactly
It’s a proof of concept that you can put chemicals together into a cell

By itself, it’s not a really good organism, but will hopefully show people that you can put together chemicals into something that can grow, divide, undergo selection, and that opens up this age of biology to me
How do these SpudCells do all of these things differently than a natural cell?  The process of eating is very similar to how bacteria and other simple cells eat

title: It shouldn’t feel impossible to finish a book
excerpt: A horror story of sorts is unfolding in the United States
body: A horror story of sorts is unfolding in the United States

It goes like this: AI has made it so effortless to access information, and short-form video has made it so easy to entertain ourselves , that nobody reads anymore.  If you’re familiar with this tale, it’s possible, ironically, that you read about it

A viral Atlantic story from earlier this summer put a chilling headline on trend: “ The End of Reading Is Here .” Teachers and professors, the magazine reported, don’t even bother assigning entire books to their students, because excerpts are good enough to prepare for standardized texts
The piece said we’re living in a “postliterate era.” This is a cultural crisis, yes — but for a lot of us, it’s a personal one

We’re all short on time, and we’d like to read more, but the ascendancy of attention-stealing tech companies has made it feel like we have less of it. “Reading was and is a crime of opportunity,” said Leah Price , a professor of modern book history at Oxford and the author of What We Talk About When We Talk About Books . “The limiting factor isn’t reading matter, but reading time.” Key takeaways Reading is changing, not dying
The bigger problem is competition for people’s time and attention
E-readers and audiobooks make reading easier, but the friction of print promotes deeper comprehension
Leisure reading should be fun! It’s totally fine to peek at the ending, skip boring parts, or just give up on boring books
Losing the reading habit is especially bad because it’s a healthy practice in a world obsessed with self-improvement
Studies suggest that reading is an astonishingly good mental exercise, as well as a very accessible one
Reading, especially leisure reading, can improve your language skills
It exposes you to new knowledge and ideas
Reading can help relieve stress, anxiety , and insomnia
It can make you more empathetic and combat cognitive decline
Reading, perhaps above all, also happens to be fun
There are, I’m happy to say, some bright spots in this story — and some helpful news
A 2025 Pew study found that the number of Americans who say they read books has remained roughly the same in recent years, although the way that they read them is changing
The vast majority of books read in the United States are print, but a growing number of people are reading e-books and listening to audiobooks
The number of print books sold is actually growing on the backs of the science fiction and self-help genres
The number of e-books and audiobooks borrowed from their local libraries, meanwhile, topped 820 million last year , a new record
And it’s never been easier to access any book you want in your preferred format
The other bit of good news is useful to you: Reading is like a muscle
Even if you feel like your ability to pore over a book has atrophied, that muscle is still there, ready for exercise
The more you do read, the more your vocabulary improves, the more you learn, and the more you’re able to put new information in context
In other words, the more you read, the better you get at it
And probably as a result, the less appealing algorithmic feeds become.  It’s one of those personal habits that extends beyond your own life, too
Becoming a better reader is good for American society
The nation’s founders believed that an informed citizenry was necessary to preserve democracy — and to prevent tyranny
A nation of people passively flipping through 10-second videos on a smartphone or bedrotting with a streaming show can be informed in a sense

You might want to be a better American.   The big question, then, is: How does one become a better reader in an era that increasingly appears to be postliterate? Actually, there are some interesting insights — and ironically, some technology — that can help
Reduce friction One thing that keeps a lot of people from reading is simply friction
Reading can be hard — or at least effortful — for a lot of different reasons.  For me, I hit friction every time I pick up all 1,300 dense pages of The Power Broker by Robert Caro
It’s the weight of a doorstop in my hands, as I struggle with the context of mid-century New York bureaucratic history, ultimately unsure if I’ll live long enough to reach the end of the book
Reading is full of friction, and finding ways to reduce friction is one way to read better
Just take the growth in e-book popularity as proof
Whereas people over 65 have historically read more than young people, more than 40 percent of young people have read an e-book in the past year, according to an April Pew study
Once you get used to the lack of pages and paper, e-readers are incredibly convenient
The classic Kindle Paperwhite is more portable than a doorstop, and you can keep an entire library on something the size of a side plate
It’s even waterproof, or at least more waterproof than paper
More advanced devices, like the Kobo Libre Colour , offer color e-ink displays and the ability to scribble on the page

title: Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.
excerpt: Fertilizer prices are on a wild ride : The war in Iran has sent fertilizer costs soaring — urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) hit $850 per metric ton i
body: Fertilizer prices are on a wild ride : The war in Iran has sent fertilizer costs soaring — urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) hit $850 per metric ton in April, 80% higher than pre-conflict levels
Prices have come down somewhat but could stay elevated through 2028
The fossil fuel problem runs deep : Natural gas isn't just used to power fertilizer production — it's a core chemical ingredient, meaning every energy price spike hits farmers

Microbes might offer some relief : Companies like Pivot Bio and Switch Bioworks are using genetically edited microbes to partly replace synthetic fertilizers — and unlike chemical alternatives, their prices don't swing with natural gas markets. " data-chronoton-post-id="1143320" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> If you’ve had to fill up your vehicle’s gas tank or buy a plane ticket lately, you’ve probably felt the effects of rising fossil-fuel prices
But farmers buying fertilizer for their crops are especially aware of just how far the ripple effects of the conflict in Iran have spread
Fertilizer prices have been on a roller coaster this year, kicked off in part by trade disruptions and high prices for natural gas, a key ingredient in fertilizer production
Let’s take a closer look at why conventional fertilizer prices are so sky-high, and how a few more climate-friendly alternatives could bring farmers some relief
As fossil-fuel prices go up, nearly all industries are affected, since most of our economy relies on these fuels to move goods and people around
But fertilizer is even more intertwined with these fluctuations, because natural gas is used as both an energy source and a chemical input in the production of ammonia, a key fertilizer ingredient

So as natural-gas prices have spiked in recent months because of the war in Iran, fertilizer prices have followed . (It’s worth briefly noting here that fertilizer production is also a major source of greenhouse-gas emissions, accounting for about 2% of the global total.) Fertilizer trade is being directly affected as well, since about one-third of global seaborne trade in fertilizers passes through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed to commercial traffic because of the conflict
Access to fertilizer could get worse for some of the poorest countries around the world because of the strait’s closure, according to a report from the World Bank
While the US largely meets demand for nitrogen fertilizers with domestic production, some imports do come from the Persian Gulf
At one point in April, the price of urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) climbed above $850 per metric ton
That’s 80% higher than it was before the conflict and the highest level since 2022, when the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the resulting conflict caused fertilizer costs to hit record highs

Prices have come down significantly, but forecasts remain uncertain. “There’s just this out-of-control supply chain that’s a lot more volatile than it’s ever been,” says Travis Frey, chief technology officer of Pivot Bio, a company making fertilizer with genetically edited microbes. (For more on these microbes, how they work, and what research is still needed, check out my latest story here .) Pivot says its products are cost-competitive with chemical fertilizers today
And because they don’t use natural gas as an input, they aren’t subject to the same price spikes
When the war in Iran started, Pivot increased the volume it planned to produce, dropped prices, and allowed farmers to lock in prices for three years, Frey says
That could be a major help for those farmers, because high prices could be here to stay for a while
Some fertilizer prices could remain high through at least 2028, according to a report from CoBank, one of the largest banks for the agriculture industry in the US
That’s partly because the war has caused long-lasting damage: 31 ammonia plants in the Middle East have been affected or shut down completely
That’s on top of 20 ammonia plants that have been damaged in Russia in recent years

Ongoing high prices can be extremely challenging for farmers. “The fertilizer price spikes, and because farmers have paper-thin margins, this is a real problem,” says Tim Schnabel, founder and CEO of Switch Bioworks, another company working on advanced microbe fertilizers
Higher costs can help push food prices higher, causing all of us to pay more at the grocery store. (It’s not just fertilizer, by the way
Farmers are also getting hit with wild diesel prices this year.) As long as we’re relying on fertilizers made with fossil fuels, food prices will be tied up with energy prices
Switch and Pivot are among the companies looking to make alternative fertilizers that use microbes to provide nitrogen to plants

There’s a limit to how much synthetic fertilizers these products can actually replace: Depending on the crop and conditions, Pivot says, its products can replace about 25% of synthetic fertilizer today, and the company hopes to reach 40% to 50% of the total

But these alternatives could be a start to untangling fossil fuels and food. “We can’t keep doing it like this,” Switch’s Schnabel says. “There’s no way we can build a society where the basis of the food chain depends on fossil fuels.” This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: Scaling agentic AI pilots across the enterprise
excerpt: As agentic AI moves from experimentation toward enterprise deployment, the challenge is figuring out how agents can work together, connect to the systems and da
body: As agentic AI moves from experimentation toward enterprise deployment, the challenge is figuring out how agents can work together, connect to the systems and data they need, and operate safely across the workflows that run a business
Although agentic AI has been adopted by some 80% of Fortune 500 companies, progress toward meaningful scale remains uneven, with many organizations still working through isolated pilots

WATCH THE WEBCAST For Arun Chandra, chief operating officer at NiCE, the first step is moving beyond experimentation for its own sake. “Everybody’s trying to figure out what can we do with this technology?” he says

But scaling requires a clearer connection to business strategy: Organizations need to define whether they are trying to increase revenue, reduce costs, or pursue another strategic or financial objective

From there, they need to rethink the workflows where agents will operate instead of just layering AI onto existing processes. “The last thing you want to do is to apply AI on an outdated or an inefficient workflow,” Chandra says
That shift requires organizations to treat agentic AI as a cohesive system
Agents need access to the data, knowledge, and context required to make effective decisions, as well as connections to back-end systems if they are expected to take action
Fragmented information can undermine those capabilities: “The efficacy of these AI agents is purely a function of the context, the knowledge, and the data they can ingest and use,” Chandra says
The organizational implications are equally noteworthy

Scaling agents can create a new form of fragmentation if teams build isolated systems that don’t connect with one another, while governance, privacy, security, and change management become more important as agents take on more consequential work
Chandra argues that AI agents should ultimately be held to the same standards as human workers, with organizations thinking of their workforce as a combination of humans and AI agents
Looking ahead, that connected approach could enable agents to work proactively and even communicate with other agents to resolve customer needs

For organizations making the transition from pilots to scale, the priority is not to “boil the ocean,” Chandra says, but to instead build a connected strategy around high-value use cases, workflows, workforce changes, and measurable outcomes

title: The face of American feminism
excerpt: American feminist leader and author Gloria Steinem photographed in San Francisco in 1977. | Janet Fries/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a
body: American feminist leader and author Gloria Steinem photographed in San Francisco in 1977. | Janet Fries/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
Gloria Steinem — the one-woman powerhouse who, in many ways, defined modern feminism in the United States — died Wednesday at 92 after six decades of activism
Steinem was a journalist and advocate who first rose to prominence in the late 1960s, just as the women’s liberation movement exploded

She co-founded Ms. magazine, a trailblazing publication that mainstreamed once-taboo topics like sexual harassment, wage inequity, and the unfair division of household labor.  As an advocate, Steinem also led protests, worked to elect more female politicians, and lobbied for abortion rights, employment protections, and the long-deferred Equal Rights Amendment
The ERA, which would create a constitutional guarantee of equal rights for women, has never officially been adopted , despite being ratified by the required number of states

Many of the other causes Steinem championed, however, are now at least firmly part of mainstream cultural and political debate.   Later in life, as the feminist movement evolved, Steinem continued to serve as a kind of elder statesperson. (We’ll break down how exactly it evolved in just a minute.) Much of her recent writing and speaking focused — for obvious, depressing reasons — on the importance of hope and persistence in social justice movements. “Hope is a form of planning,” she told Vogue on her 90th birthday, in 2024. “If you don’t imagine what could be, you’re already defeated.” Heads up: Vox is off tomorrow and Monday for the Labor Day holiday

Go a little deeper Steinem was the single-most recognizable face of American feminism, but she represented a distinct wave of it that future generations of feminists built on

American feminism is a sprawling, evolving, multifaceted movement — and its history is often broken down into four distinct periods .  First wave: 1848 to 1920 : You might better know the feminists of this era by the name “suffragists”: The troublesome campaigners who fought for women’s right to vote
This “wave,” as it’s popularly dubbed, began with the Seneca Falls convention in New York and ended with the passage of the 19th Amendment, after which momentum died down a bit
Second wave: 1963 to the 1980s : The movement revived with the publication of Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique in 1963
It also broadened its focus beyond political rights, taking on reproductive freedom, workplace and cultural sexism, sexual harassment, and women’s financial independence
Steinem was maybe the quintessential second-wave feminist
Third wave: 1991 to the 2000s : Feminism slumped a bit in the ’80s, deflated by Reagan-era conservatism and a backlash that cast feminists as bitter, bra-burning man-haters
But the Anita Hill case in 1991 revived mainstream attention to workplace harassment, discrimination and women’s exclusion from positions of power
Fourth wave: 2008(ish) to present : The current generation of feminism places greater emphasis on intersectionality and trans inclusion
But its defining trait is probably how very online it is
The fourth wave kicked off with blogs like Jezebel and Feministing and picked up steam through hashtags like #MeToo, #TimesUp, #StandWithWendy, and #YesAllWomen
In fairness, not everyone is terribly enamored with the “waves” framework
But for those of us trying to get the gist of recent history — or to take stock of what has and hasn’t changed, on the occasion of Steinem’s death — it can be a helpful way to get oriented
Vox has lots of further reading if you want to get into the nuances
