title: The Jewish Democrats trying to get to “yes” on Abdul El-Sayed
excerpt: Abdul El-Sayed, US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, leaves the stage after speaking during the state Democratic Party's nominating convention on Augus
body: Abdul El-Sayed, US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, leaves the stage after speaking during the state Democratic Party's nominating convention on August 29, 2026 in Lansing, Michigan. | Sara Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images Abdul El-Sayed is trying to win over undecided Jewish voters in Michigan — without compromising his substantive positions on Israel or disavowing his most radical allies.   During both his primary and general election campaigns, El-Sayed’s opponents have portrayed him as insensitive to Jewish concerns, if not outright antisemitic
These charges have often rested on falsely equating El-Sayed’s opposition to Zionism (he is not committed to Israel’s existence as a majority Jewish state) with a hostility for Jewish people
But in recent weeks, two other concerns came to the forefront
One was El-Sayed’s response to an antisemitic attack on a Michigan synagogue
In March, a 41-year-old named Ayman Mohamed Ghazali drove a truck into Temple Israel’s Jewish preschool
Days later, El-Sayed condemned the attack, while also noting that Ghazali had recently lost family members to an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon

El-Sayed suggested that these events illustrated how “hurt people hurt people” and that “violence is a cycle,” one that had led Ghazali to perpetrate “an evil act of displaced rage.” Separately, El-Sayed had campaigned with the far-left streamer Hasan Piker during his primary campaign
This had always sat poorly with many Jewish and centrist Democrats in Michigan
But Piker made his association with the Democratic Senate candidate more conspicuous in late August

During a broadcast, Piker lambasted Jeremy Moss , a pro-Israel Jewish Democrat running for Congress in Michigan who had not endorsed El-Sayed but was in active conversations with the candidate about how to bridge lingering divides with Jewish voters

More explosively, Piker said, among other things, that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually somebody is going to come around and take action, not against the State of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” He subsequently insisted he was merely spotlighting the hazards of portraying all Jews as ardent Israel supporters, not making some kind of veiled threat, as his detractors alleged

Nonetheless, this triggered a new round of calls for El-Sayed to both disavow Piker, and to take other measures to reassure Michigan Jews that he cares about their safety.  These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally

But he did defend the right of all Americans “to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” saying this was “particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.” Some Jewish Democrats found this insufficient
In an open letter Wednesday, 400 Democratic Jewish Michiganders — including donor Rob Orley — announced that they would be supporting Republican Mike Rogers in their state’s Senate race
Days earlier, El-Sayed had sought to mend fences with such voters at a summit held by the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus

During his appearance there, he apologized for his remarks following the Temple Israel attack, saying “I should have issued a statement, of course condemning it, and it just should have been the full stop.” Among those in attendance was Charles Gaba, a healthcare analyst and major Democratic fundraiser; Michigan state Sen
Mallory McMorrow has called him “ the biggest powerhouse democratic donor wrangler that nobody has ever heard of.” Gaba was a strong supporter of Rep
Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary
And he has expressed serious reservations about El-Sayed, even while committing to voting for him and raising money for his candidacy

These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally: over how far Democrats can and should go in criticizing Israel, whether the left takes antisemitism seriously, and if centrists are using allegations of anti-Jewish bigotry to stigmatize legitimate dissent.  To explore these debates — and clarify the concerns of “Sayed-skeptical” Jews in Michigan — I spoke with Gaba this week.   Our conversation has been edited for clarity and concision.  From your vantage point, what are undecided Jewish Michiganders’ biggest reservations about El-Sayed — and how many are actually addressable by his campaign?  I’d say that there’s probably four main ones
Two are connected to his comments about the Temple Israel attack
And he definitely addressed one of those complaints with his statement: that it was awfully timed
In other words, that days after the attack was not a good moment to raise other issues instead of simply condemning the violence full stop
But the larger issue to me — and to a lot of other folks I’ve spoken with — is he seemed to be under the impression that timing was the only problem
That it was just too soon and if he’d waited a month and then made the exact same comments about “context,” that would have been fine
He doesn’t seem to get that trying to put it in context at all is the larger problem
Because a bunch of preschoolers at a synagogue in Michigan have absolutely nothing to do with a military conflict overseas, just nothing
If a family member of someone who died in the September 11th attacks had gone and attempted to kill Muslim children, their loss wouldn’t be relevant context
You couldn’t say, “Oh well, but he was upset about that attack.”  I think an El-Sayed supporter might say: There’s a difference between explaining an abominable act and excusing it

In his original statement, El-Sayed did say explicitly that “t here is never a justification for attacking innocent people or houses of worship” and described the violence as “heinous” and “evil.” Taken literally, he was arguing that the strike that had killed Ghazali’s family members led to his act of antisemitic terrorism, even as nothing could possibly justify it.  There was just no reason to try to put it in context at all
Pretty much everyone understands that the Israel-Hamas war has brought emotions to a fever pitch for a lot of people
I don’t think we needed someone to say, “Hey, that whole mess in the Mideast might have inspired this!” Yeah, no shit
Who was the audience for this? Who was he trying to give context to? Certainly the Jewish community understands the situation
I think the Muslim community understands the situation
I don’t think it served any purpose other than to upset and offend a bunch of people
So he was lecturing to no one essentially, in my view
Which I get; I have a tendency to do that myself sometimes in other ways
And shifting the timing wouldn’t have made it helpful
So, what are the other two big sticking points for Jewish Democrats not sold on El-Sayed? The third is this Hasan Piker guy
The media certainly seems to be pretty focused on that

title: New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say
excerpt: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution
body: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago
